No, Mr. Chairman, I have no statement to make. I shall follow my usual practice of answering questions to the best of my ability.

I see that there is an amount of $35 million odd for the trans-Canada highway. That seems to me to be pretty small having in mind the amount of work that should be done on the highway each year. The minister may say it is the fault of the provinces that not enough work is being done. As I see it, the department is not doing enough work and providing enough money for this project. The highway has been under construction for some six years now and there is legislation before the house to extend the time of construction for another six years. This is a federal highway and by the end of another six years the part of the highway constructed in the first few years will be worn out unless the government takes hold of the situation and makes it a federal highway from coast to coast.
So far as the provinces are concerned, all the provinces now have more roads to look after than they can handle. There is an increase in road transportation. The number of cars has doubled in the last six years. The number of trucks has more than doubled and the weight of the loads carried by the trucks has increased. Speed of vehicles is also increasing. I am sure the minister and the government would be proud to say that we have a good trans-Canada highway but if the government wants such a highway the department must do more towards its construction. If they have not got the knowhow or the ways and means to build the trans-Canada highway they should give the provinces more money. They should pay at least 90 per cent of the total cost of the road right across the country. As I said before, if something more is not done quickly and better construction provided great portions of the highway will be worn out before the last part is completed.
The minimum width of the highway is 22 feet. Six years ago a width of 22 feet did not sound too bad, but with two lines of traffic travelling along a highway with a 22 foot top, one going east and one going west, the wheels of the vehicles run along in about the same place on the highway with the result that the highway wears out much more rapidly. I think many parts of the highway should have a 30 foot top and some parts should have four lanes.
As for the provinces putting up very much money for the building of the highway, it is not possible. I think Ontario is representative of all the provinces and Ontario has more north and south roads than it can maintain. We all know that we need north and south roads just as much-and from the provincial point of view probably more- than we need a trans-Canada highway. In

Ontario the great commercial and tourist traffic is mostly north and south because our big cities are found along the lakes and rivers in the southern part of the province. I refer to Windsor, the cities of the Niagara district, Hamilton, Toronto and, farther east, Cornwall. We must not forget Port Hope, the great uranium centre. Then we go east down the St. Lawrence where there have to be bridges across the river for north and south traffic.
Then, there is the defence aspect. In case of invasion or a bomb dropping on this country and people having to be moved out of the cities, we cannot move them over to the United States because they would be in more danger there than they would be here. We cannot move them east and west, so there is only one way to move them and that is north. There are not enough aeroplane facilities to move more than a small percentage of the people out of the cities, so there is only one way to move them and that is over our highways. If we are considering our national defence situation and the moving of people out of cities in case of emergency, then we have to have north and south roads. The provinces seem to think they are responsible for these roads. If they are, and they have been spending large sums on these north and south roads, then it is up to this government to do more towards building the trans-Canada highway. A better road should be built. You have to change the set-up from what it was six years ago and you have to build a better and wider road before it will ever be successful.
As I said, the dominion government should pay up to 90 per cent of the cost of this trans-Canada highway and should get more of the construction work done. I feel this is more the responsibility of the dominion government than it is of the provinces because in the first seven months of 1955 this government collected $116 million from the motor industry in excise and sales taxes. During the same period this government only spent $15f million on road construction, in spite of the fact they collected about seven times that amount from the motor industry.
Then, I should like to say a word about public buildings. Last year there was a lot of talk about public buildings and some debate concerning the west block. I am not going to say anything about that now because there is a specific item under which that can be discussed. Whether or not there is some responsibility in the federal district commission, I still think that a great deal of the responsibility for public buildings lies with the Department of Public Works. We have quite a collection of temporary buildings, but
Supply-Public Works they do not seem to be very temporary because they have been there for 15 years. There are some down on Mackenzie avenue. We are told that space is scarce, but you could take three of those temporary buildings and put one on top of the other and have a much better building.
There are civil servants working in these buildings, yet not one of the buildings has any provision for air conditioning. They are hot in the summer, especially the top floors, and not fit for offices. I think it is time the minister grasped the situation and did more than has been done in the past. There is no reason why these buildings should be left for another 15 years. I cannot blame this minister for more than the last couple of years in so far as this situation is concerned, or the deputy minister either. I ask the minister, when he is straightening up his department, to do something about those temporary buildings.
Then, there is the printing bureau. I cannot blame this minister for that, either. This building cost several million dollars, but when the location was chosen it was one of the worst blunders this department ever made. I do not think the blunder was made by the deputy minister or even the engineers. I believe the location was chosen by the then minister. He got paid off by a seat on the exchequer court bench, so he was very well treated for making one of the biggest blunders that has ever been made so far as buildings around Ottawa are concerned. The first year they had the thing sort of cleared out it looked more like a lake than a place on which to erect a building. If they had planted some fish in it and left them alone it would be a good tourist fishing place on the shore of the Ottawa river today. There does not seem to be any drainage, because this year the water has been backing up. The department will have to put in some new drainage system.
I also hear that some of the foundations for some of the machines are not holding up satisfactorily. I do not mean the foundations of the building, but some of the floors are not holding up well under some of the heavy machines. That is something that needs immediate consideration. I do not say you should erect a new building. The building is there. It was built in a sort of lake-swampy area. The mistake was made when that site was chosen. It was all right to build it on the other side of the river, but they could have selected higher and better ground for the building at that time. The building cost something over $13,500,000. I understand it is a long way from being completed. The department is going to have the problem of doing something

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with some interest to the remarks that have just been made in reference to some aspects of the estimates of the Department of Public Works, with reference to such matters as the trans-Canada highway, and so on. As the discussion of these estimates proceed some of my colleagues will be discussing such matters as that, but I do not intend to make any particular reference to those aspects at this time. However, I should like to make a few comments upon what I consider to be important aspects of the general picture of the Department of Public Works in the life of Canada today.
I can readily understand that while a couple of years ago the minister was willing to make some statement at the beginning of his estimates on administrative plans which he
(Mr. Hodgson.]

proposed to carry out, and which I believe he has been attempting to carry out, at this particular time he is apparently loath to give us any comprehensive statement of the operations of his department, or of the place that it should hold in the life of Canada. As I say, I can readily understand the minister's dilemma at this time because it appears to me he has been rather effectively hamstrung by the general policy of the government of which he is a member. For that reason, he is probably at something of a loss as to what he might say if he were to make an initial statement. In my humble opinion, I feel the committee has cause to extend a great deal of sympathy to the minister. I might say that my heart bleeds for him because he has been left in a position where I am sure he hardly knows whether he is standing on his head or on his feet.
Perhaps to illustrate the point of that remark I might be allowed to refer briefly to the speech which was made by his colleague, the Minister of Finance, on March 20 when he brought down his budget. I feel that some statements that were made at that time illustrate the dilemma faced by the Minister of Public Works at this time. As reported at page 2327 of Hansard of March 20, the Minister of Finance said:
The blessings of an economy operating at a high level are pleasant indeed to a minister of finance but they bring with them new responsibilities for all of us. The objective should be to maintain a steady growth in economic activity without the process of expansion giving rise to inflation and instability. Consequently, in times like the present when private expenditures are expected to rise still further, the federal government itself has a special responsibility to see that its fiscal policies continue to be directed towards economic stability.
A little later on in his speech the Minister of Finance went on in effect to expand what he said as recorded on page 2327, and on page 2330, he had this to say:
In many fields the services provided by the federal government have to expand along with the increase in population and national production. I need only mention such things as the provision of inspection services of all kinds, customs administration, trade promotion, surveys, research and the provision of transportation facilities, for example. If these services do not keep in step with public need the expansion of the economy will itself be hampered.
Well, as I listened to the Minister of Finance making that statement I must say that I found myself rather in agreement with him, but a little farther on in his speech he made a statement which I feel does illustrate the dilemma in which he

has placed his colleague, the Minister of Public Works, because he said this, at page 2331 of Hansard:
The program of public works and other capital items for the coming year has been held down to immediate essentials. The main estimates which have been tabled indicate that the appropriations proposed to cover expenditures on public works and other capital items are down by nearly $10 million from the previous year.
A little later on he said:
In proposing small expenditures for capital purposes, the government is seeking to reduce the strain on the economy resulting from the very large increase in capital expenditures which private industry is planning to make during 1956.
It struck me at the time, and I still feel my impression then was correct, after having reread the statement, that the Minister of Finance could not have more effectively contradicted himself than he did in the last two statements I have read. On the one hand he says that in an expanding economy the need for public services and the provision of facilities for the public need to be kept in line with the increase in the general economy. On the other hand, he turns around and says, "We are reducing our capital expenditures so it will not put any strain on the economy". I think that illustrates the dilemma in which the Minister of Public Works finds himself when he attempts to provide for the needs of the Canadian people in so far as the services that come under the jurisdiction of his department are concerned.
The general statement of the Minister of Finance is borne out by the figures that are recorded on the summary of standard objects of expenditure because in the public works department', under the category of construction or acquisition of buildings and works, we find the sum of $89,980,000 listed as compared with $95,678,000 that was provided in the estimates a year ago.
Just to make it clear that the item for that particular department is not out of line with the general pattern that has been established by the estimates, I might point out that the total expenditure for all departments for construction or acquisition of buildings and works, excluding the items for defence production, national defence and civil defence, is $184,905,000 for this year as compared with $187,274,000 that was provided in the estimates of last year.
The same pattern is followed in respect of items for construction or acquisition of equipment both within the Department of Public Works and in the general pattern established by the total of estimates for all departments.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in this connection the government has not only effectively contradicted itself in such policies as
Supply-Public Works it has brought forward but it has made it clear that its policy is going to be one that will be continued into the future and there will be an unsatisfied back log of services for the people of Canada.
According to the Minister of Finance and and the figures he used, our economy is expanding by something like 5 per cent per annum. It would seem to me that in view of the minister's statement on page 2330 of Hansard to the effect that the federal government's services have to expand in many fields it would have been logical to have expected that in this year's estimates there would have been something like a 5 per cent increase in the amount provided for giving these services to the people of Canada rather than a quite substantial decrease in these items as I have pointed out.
I feel that this situation does point up the necessity of some policy along the lines of planning and investment boards which hon. members in this group have consistently advocated for the past number of years. What the Canadian people need is some sort of arrangement whereby, as the economy of the country expands and the population increases, essential government services are going to keep pace with that expansion and the amounts available for capital investment should be diverted in some orderly and rational manner so there will be an intelligent division between the amount's of capital expenditures that are made available for productive plants, and the amount that is being put into the production of services and conveniences for the people who live in this country.
In the city of Port Alberni, which is the largest centre of population in my constituency, there is a rather pointed illustration of what I have been talking about. I mention it at this time simply because I feel it does illustrate a situation which is repeated dozens and probably hundreds of times across the length and breadth of this country.
I recently had sent to me by a very prominent citizen of Port Alberni, who I happen to know has never been a political supporter of mine, a clipping from one of the local papers which showed a cartoon picture of the post office clock. As he pointed out, this clock is on top of the tower of a rather ancient looking brick structure that was put there in the year 1913, a year after the city of Port Alberni was incorporated. This clock has in effect made something of a laughing stock of the Department of Public Works and has caused many citizens in that community to view with some scepticism the effectiveness of the policies and planning of this government. The clock now sits in the centre of the town as a sort of symbol of the archaic attitude of the federal government.
This particular cartoon shows a sea gull's nest on one of the top brackets of the tower. A young sea gull has suddenly become somewhat bold and is hanging down from the corner by his two feet. The mother sea gull is looking at her young one in a rather startled fashion, and the youngster says, "Lookit, ma, no hands!"
I know this does not represent the complete picture of what the department has in mind. I suppose the Department of Public Works plans some day to erect a new building, but the irony of the situation was pointed out to me by someone who, as I say, is a very prominent citizen. The clock sits there at a time when that community is growing by leaps and bounds and when something like $60 million is being spent in that community in the expansion of pulp mills and other industrial ventures.
This particular area along with some other parts of my constituency are part and parcel of the rapid expansion of this country and the buoyant economy about which the Minister of Finance spoke in such glowing terms in his budget speech. I do not doubt that the expansion in that area is far above what would be the national average. In spite of the investment of hundreds of millions of dollars, as a symbol of the dilemma in which the Minister of Public Works has been placed by the government to which he belongs, is this old brick tower with the clock on top of it without any hands.
In taking part in the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Public Works I want to plead that he be given a chance to do the kind of job I think he could do if the general policy of the government would permit. The same situation applies, not only in the field of public buildings but in the planning for such projects as a highway system in Canada and many other things which most likely will be mentioned during the course of this discussion.
According to the budget presented by the Minister of Finance, the federal government has control of the fiscal and monetary policies of the country. The budget gave us a rather extensive and complicated survey of the growth of the country. It is obvious to me that there has been no real thinking in an effort to remove the dilemma of providing public services to the people of Canada proportionately to the general expansion of our


economy. Rather than face up to the problem, at this time the government are taking steps which will simply aggravate it. We are going behind.
Because of the lead that has been given by the federal government in connection with this particular aspect of providing public services, we find the same dilemma has percolated down to the lower levels of government, to the provincial and municipal governments. We boast about the wealth and prosperity of our country and at the same time ask hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens to live in a completely unnecessary state of hardship because of a lack of services which our productive machinery is quite capable of providing.
This is simply a perpetuation of the pioneer, frontier type of economy at a time when we like to boast about the great industrial productivity now available to us. Why should we have to continue to live like those people who went out and put up sod shanties on the plains when they were trying to establish an economic foothold in that part of the country? That sort of thing should have gone by the board long ago. I have been told that when I was two years old I lived in one of those sod shanties.
If all the things the Minister of Finance tells us about our economy are true, and I do not think any hon. member would deny that we have the productive capacity in this country, given a little intelligent planning, to provide public services to keep pace with our growth. We have the basic wealth to provide those services.
That approach is recognized in one field of activity carried on by this government. The items in the estimates covering the construction and acquisition of buildings and works by the defence production, national defence and civil defence departments this year total $199,965,000, which is an increase over the figure for last year which was $172,050,000. Those are the amounts to be voted in the field of national defence to provide some of the things which are provided in the civilian field by the estimates to which I referred earlier.
I think of a good illustration of how this is carried out by the Department of National Defence. During the course of my travels last recess I had occasion to visit one of the radar defence installations in the coastal area of British Columbia. I was most interested to see that in what had been virgin wilderness there had been hewn out what one could term a model community. That community was provided with a school of two classrooms, it had a hospital with a doctor in attendance, it had roads and all

the services that one would normally expect to find in the best developed town. That community had been created almost overnight in what had been simply rock and forest. The people in that community were being provided with a good level of community services. I could not help but contrast the situation there with the situation that prevails in some of the communities in my area and in a good many of the communities across this country which I have been able to observe.
It seems to me that if the government is capable of planning an organization and providing these services for this industrial plant, if you want to call a radar station that, it should be possible to carry forward the same sort of planning across this country in the civilian field.
I realize that as we proceed to discuss these estimates there will be many items which will involve particular discussion, some by myself and some by others of my colleagues. However, I felt that I wanted to attempt to give the committee a picture of the place which I feel the Department of Public Works should occupy in the life of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I do not suppose there is any greater challenge being faced by any minister of the government than that which the Minister of Public Works must face in trying to keep the Department of Public Works in step with the growing economy of this country. I for one feel for him. I would say that there is no job more important than to keep up with expansion, especially when it is at the rate that we have in this country today. We have immigration, defence and other problems that enter into the field to take from his dollar and add to his troubles. However, possibly part of the reason for his difficulty is the fact that governments before him, which were largely Liberal-at least for 50 years they were mostly Liberal-have accentuated the problem by not having looked after it properly in past years. No matter what he is doing to rectify the position today, we are going to find more and more of these problems arising, because our progress is so phenomenal that it makes it difficult for him to keep pace. If the hands of the clock that were referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni are the least of his problems, then I am satisfied they will soon be looked after.
However, I find in my own riding, for example, that I have the trans-Canada highway crossing navigable streams, which calls for attention. On one occasion the minister mentioned to me that he thought we must
Supply-Public Works be having bridges all over British Columbia. He needs only to see the growth in that province and he will see that we certainly have the people that require them. Six major bridge constructions in the course of the present British Columbia government are more, I understand, than were built in the previous 20 years.
How many of those are toll bridges?

So long as we can cross the streams, that is the important thing, as far as I am concerned. We have other problems, such as dredging problems. We have the problems of retaining walls, of breakwaters, of housing, of public buildings, just to mention a few. These are not just localized in my area but, I am sure, occur in many other ridings as well.
The policy of bringing in the estimates at a time such as this when we have certain resolutions by the minister on the order paper which will change some of our points of view, I am sure, might be somewhat improved if we heard a statement from the minister in respect to the intention of resolutions Nos. 10 and 11 on the order paper, and I am satisfied some of the remarks that are going to be made in the course of discussing these estimates might be changed. However, it is not my intention to deal with those resolutions.
Last year I brought to the attention of the house a certain policy which I thought was fundamentally wrong. I still believe it is wrong. That is the continued rental of buildings that cost more than $2,500 a year in rent to the taxpayer when we have to improve those buildings and spend money on repairing them as well. It is not my intention at this time to take up that problem, because there is a more appropriate occasion.
I do, however, wish to continue further my discussion with respect to a problem that arose earlier in the Department of Transport estimates, one which affects this department also. That is the question of co-operation between the departments. In order to illustrate my point it is necessary to bring in a local problem in my own area which is definitely affected by the Department of Public Works. We have in the city of New Westminster an antiquated structure which was built about 1897 and subsequently was repaired, known as the Queensborough bridge. The department has from time to time denied that it has any responsibility whatsoever for the building of that bridge. Even though it does cross a navigable stream, even though it is necessary for the city of New Westminster to get permission to build a particular

Supply-Public Works type of bridge, we are continually told there is no federal responsibility for the building of that bridge, because we cannot prove precedent.
Now let us look at this matter of precedent, and I come to another problem. In the unincorporated city of White Rock, also in my own riding, there is a railway known as the Great Northern Railway, one of the major constructions in the continent, passing through that resort town. It passes along the beach, and there is a Department of Public Works wharf across the rail line. On the opposite side of that rail line is Washington avenue. Many years ago, when the wharf was built, a crossing had to be made from Washington avenue to cross the tracks to the wharf in order to get cargo on to the wharf. An application was made to the board of transport commissioners to put a warning bell there; and that was granted. At that time the board of transport commissioners ruled as a precedent that it was the responsibility of the Department of Public Works to pay for and maintain that bell.
Access to the wharf, however, was still difficult because Washington avenue is a fairly narrow road, and it had the mountain on one side of it and the rail line on the other. In order to make it more accessible, the people in White Rock, and the municipality of Surrey particularly, decided they would build an access road crossing Washington avenue which would make it possible to go along the edge of the mountain and come back up the other side and then down this fairly steep grade known as Martin street and leading right to the water. As a result of that, we had certain communications with the department, through the Department of Transport and otherwise, which denied responsibility by this same government. Here we have a case of precedent.
Just by way of illustration, I should like to read a letter from Mr. H. A. Young, the deputy minister, dated 13th April, 1955. Before I do so, however, I should' say that the old bell is worn out and it has now become necessary to replace it with a new one. Not only that, but it is also suggested that a cautionary light be placed there because, since the time of the passing of the order in council that made it necessary for the federal governing body to build this structure and have this bell placed there, White Rock has grown tremendously. Over 30,000 holidayers come there each Sunday to the beach, and that has been the average for many years. Every one of those people must cross that track and use that particular crossing. They are using that wharf also. So are the boat owners. The department recognized the value of that


wharf only a few years ago by putting out into the bay a monstrosity known as the breakwater, which is practically useless because it is too short. However, that remains for another discussion at another time. To come back to the need for the bell, and the precedent, I have here a letter, as I indicated earlier, dated 13th April, 1955, from Mr. H. A. Young, deputy minister, in respect to replacing this bell:
Our records disclose that the Department of Public Works undertook the construction of a public wharf at White Rock in 1914. Subsequently, a municipal road was built linking Martin street, in the village of White Rock, to the wharf approach. This road intersected the Great Northern Railway right of way, the municipality of Surrey receiving permission from the board to construct a level crossing at that point. In 1915 at a sitting in Vancouver, the board directed this department to pay for the installation and maintenance of a warning signal at the crossing. This order was complied with and the department has borne the annual maintenance costs since that date. Upon review, there would appear to be some doubt as to the department's responsibility in this matter.
The phraseology of that letter and the words "upon review" intrigue me because from time to time when we suggest a bridge there is no precedent that has to be reviewed. Apparently there is no need for a review. Even though New Westminster harbour has developed as it has, even though that Queens-borough bridge is opened 42 times a day, we still have this same Department of Public Works saying: We are sorry, but we cannot find a precedent.
I found a precedent with respect to the erection of a light at another place, so the department decides it is time to review the situation. Upon review it is found that an access road to this wharf was constructed and therefore it automatically becomes the responsibility of the municipality. That, Mr. Chairman, is what I mean by policy. There is a two-way policy. When it is good for me we will do it; when it is good for you we will question it. I think that should be taken into consideration by the government any time they start telling us about precedents.
Then there is a follow-up letter written by Mr. F. D Pratt. I have forgotten Mr. Pratt's official title but I believe he is in the executive branch of the Great Northern Railway. The letter is from Vancouver and is dated April 27, 1955. I should like to refer to a short portion thereof which reads as follows:
With due respect it would appear to me that the roadway crossing the railway tracks was placed for the sole purpose of giving access to the department's wharf, and that nothing further has transpired in the meantime to change the principles arrived in the original order authorizing the protection herein.

Therefore I would say it is recognized even by the Great Northern Railway that the responsibility should be that of the department. After all, if the wharf were not there there are better places for crossing the tracks. There is a crossing farther up the line for automobiles that can be used by those who transport motorboats or motors for their boats. They have another means of access, but it is necessary to have the bell because the crossing is there. The purpose of the crossing is to get to the wharf. Admittedly, 30,000 people use that crossing on a Sunday but if the crossing were not there undoubtedly another one would be constructed in its place.
The fact of the matter is that we have here a need for a certain degree of co-operation not just by the municipality, the railway and the Department of Transport but also the Department of Public Works. I have a great deal of correspondence on this matter. I do not intend to belabour the committee by reading all of it, but there was one other factor that interested me, the review of this situation. In looking into this matter I wrote to the municipal clerk of the district of Surrey, Mr. Livingstone, on January 24, 1956. I asked him four pertinent questions because I wanted to discover how the crossing had been reviewed by the Department of Public Works. I said:
In order to proceed further with this matter and to do it as expeditiously as possible, would you please let me know at your earliest convenience:
1. If the board of transport had a representative examine the crossing in question with a representative of the district of Surrey?
Mr. Livingstone replied under date of February 3, 1956, and his answer to the first question was as follows:
Yes. The board of transport had a representative examine this crossing on July 26 last year. Mr. C ,D. Midwinter, district engineer of the board's Calgary division made the inspection, and he was accompanied by Mr. Furiak, municipal superintendent of public works.
This was my second question:
Was there present another member of the Department of Transport?
Mr. Livingstone replied:
I do not know whether or not any other member of the Department of Transport was present.
My third question was:
Was there present a member of the Great Northern Railway Company?
The answer was:
Yes. I understand the signals engineer was at this inspection.
My fourth question was:
And finally, was the Department of Public Works represented, and if so, by whom?

The answer was:
The Department of Public Works was not represented to my knowledge.
I question this type of action, Mr. Chairman. It was the responsibility of the Department of Public Works as determined in 1914 to erect this bell. There was a precedent, and now the department decides that it has no further interest in the matter even though they have maintained the bell until the present moment. The old bell is still in operation and definitely should be replaced as soon as possible. The summer season is beginning. The beach is again going to be used by thousands of people. People may possibly be injured or maimed. There was a death there a couple of years ago involving a young child who was crossing the tracks or on the tracks. There was no responsibility on the part of this particular department because the bell was in operation. However, the fact remains that it is somebody's responsibility.
This matter has been studied now for two years, and we are being told now that even though a precedent was established there is no responsibility as far as the Department of Public Works is concerned with respect to replacing the bell. As far as I am concerned, I take exception to that stand. We have a Department of Public Works which is undoubtedly doing its best to do what it thinks should be done or what it is pressed to do, possibly even for political purposes, although I should not like to charge this minister with that at this time and will not do so unless I discover that there is some real reason for an official of the department not being present at that meeting.
It would appear to me that if there was direction from the Department of Public Works here or from the Vancouver office that no one should be in attendance when the meeting was held then there must be some reasonable reason for that stand. As far as I am concerned, I can see no excuse for the department not paying the "full shot", if I may use that phrase, for the replacement of the bell. The precedent is there. It is established. The fact of the matter is that if Martin road were closed by the municipality of Surrey the crossing would still be there. That seems to be the only argument for it. Martin road was built after the crossing was constructed. It was put there for a purpose, to make access to the wharf much more simple. I think that in this particular instance the policy to break precedent is not very well founded.
There are many other problems that could be dealt with. I have one or two of a minor nature that do not appear in the estimates, but I do not wish to spend too much time

Supply-Public Works discussing them now. It might be that later on we shall find some more appropriate occasion.
However, there is one question that was dealt with when the dikes gave way in 1948 and 1952, when a certain amount of rocking was done along the Fraser river. In the Canoe pass section across from Westham island, there was a certain stretch of rocking that was not done because it was inaccessible.
I believe the B.C. Packers had a cannery at that point which made it impossible to try to do the rocking. However, that old plant has been torn down or is being torn down, and it is now possible to get to that point. We have lost a good portion of the foreshore there-I do not know exactly how many feet-but about 1,500 feet of rocking remains to be done. I would say that this work should not be left undone because in a couple of years it will cost us twice as much to do that rocking as it would now.
While I am on this subject of rocking, I wonder whether it would not be feasible, instead of using rock, to possibly use old wrecked car bodies that are available in the lower mainland. There are a lot of old cars there which the wrecking industry is not able to use. There is not a sufficient amount realized from them as scrap. I am given to understand that the municipalities have been able to arrange with these men that these car bodies be available for such purposes. These old cars would be serving a worth-while purpose if they kept the Fraser river from ravaging the lower mainland.
Added to that, I have just one other point I should like to bring to the minister's attention and that concerns the Boundary bay area. The wind and tide sweeps across to the north and hits what is commonly known as the Beach Grove resort. Considerable damage has been done each year, and it is getting progressively worse. Now, about 20 years ago on the United States side of the boundary a wooden retaining wall about 4 or 5 feet high was built. This has adequately taken care of the problem. It has been suggested that this matter be examined by the department with a view to discovering whether or not a program of continuing the wall to about half a mile past the Herd road to the north would be practical and save greater expenditure at a later date. The point is, Mr. Chairman, that we did not use these beaches years ago to the extent they are being used today. Our population was not nearly so great. Beach Grove has grown into quite a community at this time and the area does require some protection. During the winter months the wind and tides wreak a great deal of havoc in that particular area. The people have a right to expect some assistance.

During the Easter recess while touring my constituency I discovered that a great number of the inhabitants had done something about it. Some of them had gone so far as to put up their own cement retaining wall. However, it was not buttressed to any other wall, with the result that the whole area dropped back into the sea. I should like to have the minister make an examination there to see if something cannot be done, either by the department itself or in co-operation with the people in the community, to help them keep their homes and solve this problem.

I am very happy indeed to take part in this debate, for reasons which I will illustrate. I belong to a large group of people who are very happy to have the Hon. Bob Winters as Minister of Public Works. He does not need any sympathy for the job he is doing, because he is doing his job according to the tools that he has used in his profession and which I used during several years at university, namely the square, the plumbline and the spirit level. Any one who uses these tools in public buildings, or even in the ideal way, does not have to back down or knock a bulge out of a wall.
There are two things upon which I congratulate the minister in the outstanding work that he has done. The first is that he has helped us to have a trans-Canada highway. I do not need to enlarge on that. He was very patient with us in Fort William and with the provincial government. Things have been cleaned up splendidly and we are going to have a national highway that will be a credit to Canada.
The second thing upon which I congratulate him is his housing plan. I recall that when he took over that work there were numerous difficulties. We had debates in this house, and I can see him standing up and demanding a vote on his present plan. He received almost a unanimous vote. I congratulate him on the way he is handling Central Mortgage and Housing. We wish him the best kind of luck and ask him to stick to building according to his plan.
Locally, we thank him and his deputies for doing something for us which was long overdue. I tried for about 10 years to have our dredging commence as soon as the ice went out. We did not get that. Sometimes we did not get our dredging started until the first of July. When these dredging companies get their contracts they start to make their outfits ready and this takes time. The change has resulted in our dredging commencing as soon as the ice goes out. I thank the minister and his deputy very much because this is an

outstanding improvement. We do a lot of dredging at the head of the lakes, and there will be a lot more.
I have one request to make which I believe would be in the best interests of Fort William and of Canada. The Department of Labour needs a better building for the unemployment insurance offices. At the moment they are housed in the old post office. Twenty-three years ago the late Dr. Manion felt this building was not fit for a post office and a large new post office was built. This building was left empty. The deputy minister gave me the job of renting it, and I had some job. The floors were heaved and the furnace was cracked; windows were broken and the walls needed decorating and painting. I tried to get the Red Cross to take it, but they would not look at it. I tried to get the home improvement people to take it over, but they would not look at it. Finally, a group came to me and asked that it might be taken over as a beer parlour. I was not very sympathetic. Then, a group came and asked if the Salvation Army could get it and through the deputy minister, the late Mr. Hunter, we rented that building to the Salvation Army for a dollar a year.
They did a great job. Major Flesher of the Salvation Army was a fine mechanic. He fixed up the building and for seven years they had that building. I do not know whether they paid the $1 a year or not, but that does not matter. Then the war broke out and the Salvation Army had to move out. It was my job to help the Salvation Army to find another building, and we did. The unemployment insurance people took over. It is a trap. I am sure the minister agrees with me that he wants the workers to be properly protected. They are poorly protected. Any engineer would tell you that you canqot enlarge the building; there is no place to add to it. It is there on May street, and it is not a credit to us.
I must say that I am not an outstanding builder. As I said, I spent seven years in construction work and I learned a little, how to figure out a blueprint and so on. We have an armoury there. It used to be the Prince of Wales hockey rink. It is a big building in the very centre of the city. The officials of national defence do not think that armoury is suitable; it is not safe, but it did not cost us very much in the first place to remodel it. That armoury should be taken over and a federal building placed there because of the need for unemployment insurance offices, and secondly, because the dominion government is paying about $33,000 a year in taxes that could be saved. The Department of National Defence officials
Supply-Public Works want a new armoury out on what we call the Chappies Limited ground, an excellent spot. It is a good place for an armoury. I recommend it highly because we need a federal building. I am not so sure that we need an armoury because there may not be war, but if any place in Canada needs an armoury it is a place like Fort William. I make this request in all honesty and sincerity.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot very well follow in the same tone as that used by the hon. member for Fort William because I am sitting in the opposition and he is on the government side of the house. Yet I think the things he said about the minister were well warranted. I would not go as far as he did, but I will say that the Minister of Public Works stands very high in my estimation as a minister.
I want to go back to where I left off last year and speak about the breakwater at Gimli. We have not made any headway there. The minister was kind enough to make arrangements for a meeting. Well, it took three months to get that meeting going, and when we did get it going it did not do us any good. At that meeting we decided that we would have a small delegation consisting of the chamber of commerce, the mayor of the town and different individuals, meet with the engineer. Well, that meeting has never taken place. It is about a year since I spoke to the minister about it. The meeting with the engineer was arranged and 21 people came from Gimli. It is a very important topic to those people. Some of them have put their life savings in their houses, and they are watching their back yards going, and the foundations of their houses going, and I do not know how far it is going to be allowed to go.
The next thing that happened was that I received a copy of my local paper and I found a full-page advertisement of the agreements with Gimli and with the different people. I do not know why the advertisement was placed in the paper.
Who inserted the advertisement?

I do not know, but the editor had this to say in an editorial note:
The agreements published by this newspaper last December appeared as paid advertising and are not to be construed as a reflection of editorial opinion.
I do not know how much it cost the department.

Is there any reason to believe that the department did it?

Who would do it if the department did not? They were the only people who put up an argument. Perhaps the minister will find out. I will not say any more about it. Let the minister find out whether some individual paid for it, and if he did I will take back everything I said about the department. I am not going to say any more about it. Dr. Johnson was annoyed about it. He was the president of the chamber of commerce at that time. I should like to read this letter which appeared in the Selkirk Enterprise on Wednesday, February 8, 1956:
On December 29, 1955, one full page of your newspaper dealt with an agreement between the town of Gimll and the crown, concerning the Gimli shoreline.
This agreement was signed by our town council under the pressure of either sign or get no protection. Without the breakwater, our town would be practically under water.
The Gimli chamber of commerce, members of town council and ratepayers recently met with the district engineer in Winnipeg. The Gimli delegation maintained that this breakwater or shoreline is deteriorating rapidly, due to faulty construction. The government maintains if we had backfilled properly it would stand up. Individual ratepayers have backfilled at great expense to themselves and, even so, the wall is crumbling. There is no place for the water to go, once it comes over the wall, nor is there anything to break the force of the sheets of water against the flat wall in a storm.
Much negotiating has gone on, and the Minister of Public Works arranged the meeting in December inviting our ratepayers, etc. Despite the Gimli charges of faulty construction, the district engineer persisted in stating that the town of Gimli and the ratepayers had not backfilled. No answer was given to charges of faulty construction. For example, one ratepayer points out that behind his property the breakwater was anchored to a large cement slab under his fish shed. The foundation is now in lake Winnipeg. His loss he estimates is $600. Years ago in 1908 the federal government built a shoreline of wooden piles, the first of the Gimli shoreline. It lasted 20 years because wooden piles and rocks were placed out in front of the shoreline to break the waves and water did not build up behind the shoreline. This wooden edifice is cracking, sinking and shortly will crumble.
Despite these facts, we are told the story- "inadequate backfill". The district engineer agreed that our mayor had no choice but to sign the agreement-if he had not-Gimli would have been partially under water since 1951.
We feel that given a free hand and allowed to backfill, the engineer could have done the job. I am sure they felt it should be done. The agreement has been carried out by the town of Gimli and ratepayers. To "adequately backfill" this shoreline cannot be done.
The agreement published in your newspaper aggravated the people in Gimli. It was a "poor show" and I for one would like you to name the responsible party.
Surely a democratic newspaper such as yours will get behind the people of Gimli and bring forth justice before pettiness.
I cannot talk about breakwaters because I do not know very much about them; I am not an engineer. The breakwaters on the coast of Scotland always had outlets which


permitted the water to run back into the sea. This one has no outlets at all and you have only to go there and see the big waves going over to realize they would wash anything away. The shoreline there was backfilled. I have to believe what the people I represent tell me. They tell me it was backfilled and it has been washed away.
Perhaps there should have been outlets. I think perhaps the wrong type of breakwater may have been built; I say may have been built. There should have been outlets along there to let the water run back into the lake. There is nothing there but a solid wall. The waves come up and wash away any backfill that is there. I do not want to labour the point but I would like you to look into it again and see what can be done. These good people are not asking something that is unreasonable. They signed an agreement to the effect that they would keep it up but the thing was gone before they ever had a chance to keep it up. If you will look into it again I would be very pleased.
Down the lake a bit we have the town of Winnipeg Beach. I wrote to you about that and you were good enough to permit me to make arrangements with the district engineer. I met him in Winnipeg and discussed the matter and then I went back to the Winnipeg Beach council and told them that the Department of Public Works had no responsibility in the matter. The district engineer told me he had it in black and white that the town of Winnipeg Beach signed the agreement to maintain it.
I am going to read the minister another letter. I could not get anywhere. I came to the Department of Public Works for guidance in the matter because I did not know the facts. I told them that at the time. The letter I have in my hand is from Mr. L. E. Tapper, a councillor. I met him and the mayor before I came away and I got him to put it in black and white so I would not make any mistake. His letter reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Bryce:

The situation was aggravated due to the fact that the retaining wall built last winter by the dominion government, fell short of roughly 50 feet to where it should have ended and the water and sand came around the end and washed away the planking and damaged the foundation. Because of this lag

of 50 feet we find that work is in progress now and they are extending this wall some 250 feet and with extra reinforcement all the way through.
From the foregoing it is obvious that certain fault lies with the dominion government. The walkway has buckled in a number of places and I know for a fact that one particular small section has buckled at an angle of almost 45 degrees both right and left in a very short space. In certain spots new stringers and risers are necessary.
Now that the retaining wall has been extended it is an excellent time for the dominion government to come to our help and completely rebuild the walkway and planking. The damage is too great for us to suffer ourselves particularly since it is not our fault.
If the work is done early this spring as soon as conditions warrant, but long before the season opens, I am sure I could get an agreement passed by council for the future maintenance and upkeep. We feel very strongly about this as any temporary repair work would not only be expensive to us but would be thrown out money unless the job was practically rebuilt.
I might mention that I spoke to the local engineer (federal) who is in charge of the present project at the Beach and he tells me the men will be on the job another few weeks anyway as conditions this winter were not conducive to too much work being done so far.
Remember please, that this area is a great tourist attraction and people go there from all over the country and from a number of states. Unless something is done for us I know that people will stop coming. I am sure that the government does not want that to happen.
That describes the situation at Winnipeg Beach. The two big fellows are Gimli and Winnipeg Beach. I would like the minister to suggest to his engineers that they give some consideration to this.
I have only one other complaint and it is a matter which I took up last year. I refer to the different ways of messing by dredges and the Bradbury. It is still the same as it was. I think that should be straightened up; treat them all alike. There are two different systems. These fellows only work five days on the dredges and when they come home on Friday night there is still no allowance made for that. They are allowed $47 a month which amounts to about $1.54 a day. I put this matter on the record last year. I would like the minister to be good enough to look into the situation and see if he can correct it and make these people into one happy family.

At that time I expressed the hope that the present minister would improve the situation in regard to the voting of sums for public buildings and would see to it that something was done in connection with the matter, but unfortunately that has not been the situation.
I would just refer first of all to a discussion we had on April 9, 1954, in regard to a particular public building. The discussion is found at page 3971 of Hansard tor that date.
I asked the minister for what public building in Calgary there was a vote amounting to $150,000. He replied that this amount was required toward the construction of a public building in Calgary to provide improved accommodation for the Department of Veterans Affairs and other government services. I then asked the minister if this was the same building for which votes were passed in 1947-48 and in 1948-49 and whether something definite was actually going to be done in regard to the matter. At that time the minister replied:
The Department of Veterans Affairs has requested us to erect a new building on a site which is owned by them opposite the Colonel Belcher hospital.
It is our intention to proceed with the erection of a building on that site. The plans are not yet beyond the preliminary stage and I am not in a position to say when the building will be started.
Nothing was done in connection with that matter in 1954. In last year's estimates this same amount of $150,000 appeared as a revote. Once more nothing was done in regard to this matter. I notice that the vote has been dropped altogether in this year's estimates; it does not appear at all. In other words we have had an exact repetition of what occurred back in 1947, 1948 and 1949. The vote appears for two years, or in some cases three years, nothing is done in connection with the matter and then it disappears from the estimates book altogether.
The history of the past ten years as far as the erection of public buildings in Calgary is concerned has been a most unfortunate one. I went into it in detail at that time, but I shall just recapitulate what has happened. During the period 1947 to 1956 inclusive the amounts voted for public buildings in Calgary totalled $849,500; there were revotes amounting to $466,500, so that the votes in connection with which one might have expected something to be done would total $383,000. However, there was nothing like that amount of building done. Included in that total is this vote of $150,000 which was in the estimates for last year and which has now been dropped. If we subtract that amount we have left a total of $233,000.
As I say, there was a vote of $100,000 for this building back in the 1949 estimates.

Supply-Public Works Evidently it was put in there at that time for election purposes and as soon as the election was over the vote was dropped. As far as I can find out, without having the figures before me and having to depend only upon the books of estimates, the actual amount spent out of the $849,500 for public buildings in Calgary was $133,000 as a maximum.
I submit that this method of estimating and carrying on business is extremely unsatisfactory. It is the old business of holding out a carrot for a certain length of time, taking it away, putting it out again, taking it away, and so on. Nobody knows what the situation is, whether a building is going to be built, or what is going to happen. We have been dangled along in Calgary for ten years in regard to public buildings. Votes have appeared in the estimates at various times during this period and the Minister of Public Works has said that they were going to proceed with buildings, but nothing has started. This goes on year after year and then the whole thing is dropped.
This particular item was dropped after having been there for the last two years. It was dropped following 1949 after having been there for two years. I wonder if the government is ever going to build this building. There is no question of the necessity of a veterans building in Calgary. The offices of the Department of Veterans Affairs are scattered among four or five buildings. They have a few offices in the Michael building, a few offices in what used to be Garbutt's business college, a few offices in the Belcher hospital and so on. This makes it extremely inconvenient for the veterans and other people in Calgary who are forced to run around from one office to another. These offices are some considerable distance apart.
This must prove to be inconvenient and expensive as far as the Department of Veterans Affairs is concerned through having to carry on business in that way. However, the great complaint is of the inconvenience and time lost by veterans and other people who must make use of these facilities.
In addition, there is a great need for office accommodation in Calgary for other governmental departments. The income tax branch and certain other offices are in the Traders building, an old department store. There have been complaints about the location of these offices, their inconvenience and so on. These complaints have been coming in for many years but nothing has been done. I wonder how long this sort of thing is going to continue and whether a definite provision is going to be made for a public


building in Calgary. I wonder whether construction will actually be started as long as this government is in office.
I might just point out, as I pointed out in 1954, that during this same period the amount voted for public buildings in Edmonton was over ten times the amount voted for public buildings in Calgary. I have not computed the actual amount spent in Edmonton but it must be twenty or thirty times as much. There seems to be no rhyme or reason to the way the construction of public buildings in the province of Alberta is carried out.
I assume that in this particular case the estimates next year, immediately before the election which we are reasonably sure will come then, will again contain this item for $150,000, or it may even be for $1 million. It does not matter how much is put in as long as nothing is going to be spent. If you are the Minister of Public Works you might as well be a good fellow and put in an item for $5 million or $10 million. As long as nothing is going to be spent it does not really make much difference what figures are contained in the estimates book.
There is another public buildings project in Calgary which has received a great deal of attention. I refer to the new post office building. According to the Calgary newspapers, either the Post Office Department or the Department of Public Works had entered into negotiations for a site along the C.P.R. tracks. That was something over a year ago and we have had no further information on the matter. There is nothing in the estimates this year for that building.
I think the time is long overdue when the minister should put an end to this situation. Two years ago I began to hope that he would do so, but so far his record is no better than that of the previous minister so far as public buildings in Calgary are concerned. I should like to have him make some definite statement in connection with this matter before these estimates are completed.

I can truthfully say that my employment with the Department of Public Works of Canada on one occasion caused me 15 minutes of the most extreme anguish that I have ever suffered in my life. On one occasion an engineer in charge of the construction of a wharf some few miles north of my home was taken ill. The district engineer, who knew me, said he thought I looked intelligent enough to replace him to carry on the construction of the wharf. Years ago the Department of Public Works of Canada had quite an establishment in Nelson. It had a district office, and several engineers worked from that office. Since that time we have just had occasional visits from engineers from the office in New Westminster who now flit in and flit out of our part of the country like bats going in and out of a belfry. This is a very different set of circumstances from that which existed in the early days. When I was a boy the district engineer and the other engineers made a point of attending farmers' institute meetings and meetings of local organizations, seeking advice and discussing with those present certain problems in connection with wharves and dredging and things of that sort. Whilst very few of these people had engineering experience, there is a knowledge of local conditions that is gained as a result of living in a certain area, which is superior to the knowledge that a person may have with much greater technical training who flits in and out of the area on periodic visits. Another matter which I wish to draw to the attention of the minister is the erection of a federal penitentiary in Drumheller. It is my understanding, and in fact the information was made public, that three penitentiaries will be built in western Canada. I have been informed that the people of Drumheller have communicated with the minister in this regard and have pointed out to him the advantages of having a penitentiary located there.
Once again I am sure the minister's good judgment will prevail. Upon close inspection I am sure that he will find there is no better place to build a penitentiary than in Drumheller. It is an ideal location and is served by the railway. It has a first-class hardsurfaced highway which passes through Drumheller going from Calgary out to the Saskatchewan border. It is an exceptionally good agricultural area. I am sure the minister will be impressed when he examines the possibility of locating the penitentiary there.
This is not a case of asking for more money to be spent on public works projects. I am merely pointing out to the minister that a certain sum of money is going to be spent and it is just a matter of selecting the most suitable location. If the minister together with his engineers will examine this proposition carefully I am sure his good judgment will again prevail.
I mentioned in my opening remarks that we in Bow River have not very much to complain about. I am sure I am too modest to say that that is because I have been the member for that constituency and that that is the reason so many of these projects in Bow River have been developed.
There is another thing which I should like to draw to the attention of the minister and which I am sure will meet with his approval.
I refer to the need of a civic centre in Banff. In bringing this up I may be transgressing


upon the jurisdiction of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, but I do make this appeal to the minister because of his exceptionally good judgment in such matters.
I believe it has been suggested to the minister that the cost of such civic centre should be financed partly by the people of that area. I take objection to that because I do not believe that the 2,500 people in Banff should be asked to carry fifty per cent of the financial burden entailed by the erection of such a building. If this building is of the type of other buildings that have been built in Banff, and I do not think it would be the desire of the minister or anyone else to have an inferior building, it will cost a considerable sum. I do not think the local people should be asked to finance such a large expenditure as would be involved.
This building should be of such a type that it will be an asset, not only because of the accommodation it provides but for its scenic appearance. This is a national park and this should be a national attraction. It is hoped that when the building is built it will be able to accommodate national conventions which would be something worth while. I would point out the urgency in respect to national participation. It should not be left to the local people to finance even a portion of the cost of such a structure.
I should like to hear the minister's comments on this. I am sure he has given this matter some consideration. I do not expect that there will be an item in the supplementary estimates this year, but if it is given the consideration it deserves I would hope to see an item next year to cover the construction of such a worth-while project as a civic centre in our leading Canadian national park.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with those who have spoken in congratulating the minister upon the improvement in his department since he has taken over. The political skulduggery in the department has not all disappeared so I do not want the minister to become too complacent. I believe there is some there yet.
I have been pressing the minister for some years for an annex to the post office building in Exeter. This is needed very badly. I notice there is an item of $50,000 to cover this and I hope that is not simply a book item. That building should be started and if possible completed this year. I should like the minister to indicate whether it will be gone ahead with this summer as it has been needed for some time.
In 1953 we understood that a post office building was to be erected in Hensall. The

site was supposed to have been bought and a building was to be erected and rented to the Post Office Department for ten years. However something apparently got into the machinery and the item disappeared and the result is that we still have no post office building. This lively town has grown considerably in the last few years and needs a post office building very badly. I ask the minister to remember this and perhaps next year we will see something for a post office building in Hensall.
Then I should like to say something about the post office in Brussels. That post office is a very good one and there is a lovely apartment upstairs. I have spoken to the minister about this and I do not blame him entirely for what happened. A family came to that town intending to build a house and they asked to rent the apartment which was the only one available with heavy wiring to permit the use of the equipment they had. The apartment had been empty for some years. I went to the minister and he very graciously consented to allow this family to move in until such time as their house was completed.
However, there were a few political heelers around there who did not want anybody else in this apartment when they could not get it themselves and these people were told to get out. They would have stayed for two months longer and as a result the department would have made another $100 if these people had not been asked to vacate. That is what I call political skulduggery and I do not think the minister should allow that sort of thing to happen. The department has been beaten out of $100 which they could have had. These people were good tenants and would have stayed until their house was completed. But they had to move out of the apartment and into their house before it had much more than a roof on it.
These are a few of the things I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister. While I realize that his department is running much more efficiently than it was before his time, I think there is still room for improvement and the minister should not become too complacent.

Mr. Chairman, I want to join with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in his reference to the necessity for action being taken to overcome hazards created by slum dwellings which have taken such a terrible toll of life in Ottawa in recent months. I should like to have the minister reply, realizing that this is a national problem, and indicate why the national government should not give a lead by convening a conference with the provinces 67509-185J
Supply-Public Works and municipalities to consider the adoption of an effective slum clearance program throughout the dominion. Such a program would pay dividends in the way of saved lives and also in the reductions that would take place in insurance problems. I commend the hon. member for the suggestion he has made. I think it is a federal responsibility, particularly in Ottawa, which is our national capital.
I do not rise for the purpose of making a plea for extra expenditures in my constituency although I can think of many things I should like to have done. On this occasion I should like to deal with what the Department of Public Works has done in connection with the building of the dominion bureau of statistics building and the printing bureau building. I can think of no other institution that equals that printing bureau for spongelike efficiency in using up dollars. It has a record unequalled anywhere, I think, for expenditure that is difficult to justify.
However, I am going to speak of white elephants in general. In the expenditure of money by the Department of Public Works I would take it that a desirable end would be economy with efficiency. Some time ago I asked a question in connection with the dominion bureau of statistics building, and I found that it was completed in 1952 and occupied on January 14, 1953. Complaints had been received from those members of the civil service who occupied it because of its draftiness and also its general lack of heat. In consequence of those complaints, in a matter of only two or three years after the completion of this building, $82,900 was expended to cover storm windows additional to those provided for in the original agreement.
I do not know whose responsibility it was, and I should like the minister to explain. Was it a failure on the part of the architects or those who did the planning in the Department of Public Works, or was it a failure on the part of the contractors? In the past few days I have heard complaints regarding this building; not only that many of the employees there suffer from excessive cold in the wintertime, but that in the summertime they suffer from excessive heat and even in the wintertime, in the two wings, those who occupy those areas find themselves subjected to excessive heat up to 90 degrees, because of the necessity of overheating those wings in order to make possible a reasonable heating of the other portion.
The information I have is that the heating and ventilating system is inoperative, that the metal sashes and the general expanse of windows cause the building to be hotter in
2918	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works summer than the ordinary wooden temporary buildings in Ottawa. The humidity in the building is about 20 per cent, instead of the 40 to 50 per cent recommended for office buildings during the winter. The consequence has been a higher percentage of colds and other similar illnesses than should be justified, having regard to a reasonable application of modern heating techniques.
Since in the next ten years $100 million worth of government buildings are to be built in Ottawa, I would ask the minister what is being done by his department to investigate the failures that have been evident in the bureau of statistics building, so the same mistakes will not be made again. I would like to find out from him whether there is any co-operation between the department of public health and the Department of Public Works with regard to specifications such as these; the required floor space for desks, filing cabinets, etc., that should be allotted to each employee; what should be the maximum temperature and relative humidity, in winter and in summer; to what degree has an examination of this D.B.S. building shown that reasonable regard to the needs of humidity and heat were assured: and, if that cannot be done in that building, that the lessons that were learned in connection with the building of the D.B.S. will be applied in the other buildings that are proposed to be constructed in this city and elsewhere.
Which officials approved the standards for the D.B.S., and which persons drew up those standards? Were they done after consultation with health officials and architects constructing similar buildings in this and other countries? I think questions such as these deserve to be answered so that what has taken place with regard to this building will not be multiplied with regard to the other buildings the government has in contemplation or that future governments will build within the next ten years. What investigation has been made into this building to ascertain what improvements can be effected? Will the lessons that this building has taught be sufficiently learned that they will not be reincorporated in further buildings that will be erected?
These are questions that are large enough to deserve the consideration of the minister and his officials, for certainly there is no economy in erecting a building such as the dominion bureau of statistics and then within three years finding it necessary to expend a further $88,000 because of somebody's failure at the time construction was originally proceeded with.
Finally there is one other question I should like the minister to elucidate. I And an examination has been made in the United States,


and conclusions have been drawn as a result of the hearing of evidence, on the important question of whether it is not cheaper in the long run, in the building of administrative edifices, to build small ones to accommodate 300 to 500 employees, rather than large multi-storeyed buildings to accommodate many. After all, what the department must have as its target is efficiency plus economy. What are the lessons this department has learned in the last two or three years as a result of the building of the dominion bureau of statistics and as a result of the construction of the printing bureau, which certainly does give one some conception of the meaning of "from everlasting unto everlasting."
These are things that the house and the country have a right to be fully informed on, for certainly what took place in the building of the dominion bureau of statistics deserves an explanation and at least the assurance that there will be no repetition in the future, because money wasted simply means added taxation. I advance this in a spirit of fair criticism and I ask the minister, when he replies, to let the house and the country know that the recent mistakes, which are apparent to those who occupy the buildings to which I have made reference, will not be reincorporated and continued in the erection of other buildings, not only here in Ottawa but elsewhere in Canada as well.
Mr. Chairman-

Do I understand
that if the minister speaks now he will close the debate on the first item?
