speechtext: There is no closing of the debate in committee.

There is no closing of the
debate. I would be very glad to wait until the hon. member had spoken, but it seemed to me we were getting down to a discussion of particular items. If we could dispose of the administration item we could make better progress with the appropriate officials here in our discussion of particular items concerning architecture and so on. Therefore if it is generally agreeable I will deal with the general discussion at this stage and we can then go on with the consideration of particular items.
At the outset I should like to thank all hon. members who took part in the discussion of the general item, especially, of course, those who were kind enough to speak so highly of the work of the department. I should certainly like to associate myself with them, because I feel that during the past year the officials of the department have done an extraordinarily good job of work at a time when the department was undergoing a reorganization which made their problems

somewhat more difficult than they otherwise would have been. It is gratifying to know that some hon. members at least feel that the reorganization work that has taken place has been to the benefit of the department and has reflected to the advantage of the country in the work the department has been trying to do.
I wish again to commend the critic of the official opposition on the manner of his approach to his job. This is the second year now that the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, has been the official critic with respect to the estimates of the Department of Public Works, and I welcome his comments as always. He dealt particularly with the trans-Canada highway. I think he was under one misapprehension in referring to the limit on expenditures imposed by the federal government. I think he had in mind that the $20 million shown in the estimates was the limit of expenditure that the federal government was authorized to make in any one year. That is not the case. The amount the department is authorized to spend is the statutory amount running to a total of $150 million. This is simply a matter of budgeting, and it does not impose a limitation.
The fact of the matter is we would be only too happy if the provincial governments could spend at least the amount for which we have budgeted, and if they could exceed that amount we would be happy and more than gratified to make the money available. My hon. friend referred to the standard of the highway as being somewhat minimum in the light of present traffic developments. I, of course, agree with him in that regard. The optimum standard specified in the agreement is a 24-foot paved top with 10-foot shoulders on both sides, and our difficulty has been to persuade the provincial governments to live up even to that standard. Most of them have advocated and insisted, in many cases with merit, that the road should be narrower having regard to the volume of traffic it will carry in anything like the foreseeable future.
The province of Ontario, for example, has insisted very strongly on a 22-foot paved surface despite our own views that a 24-foot wide paved surface would be much better. I do not believe in the case of Ontario, to which my hon. friend referred in particular, that the limitation is money more than anything else. Construction problems have been difficult and it has been a matter of decision with the Ontario government as to which highways they would assign priority.
The fact remains that they undertook by agreement with us to complete their portion
Supply-Public Works of the highway by the end of the current calendar year. This will not be done in Ontario, and it will not be done in any other province in Canada. For that reason we have a notice on the order paper now forecasting legislation which I hope will accelerate the pace of construction of the trans-Canada highway and conclude it on a date that I hope will be agreed upon before very long. Since the trans-Canada highway will again be before the house very shortly, perhaps we could defer a more detailed consideration of it until that time. That does not mean, of course, that I am not prepared to answer questions now, because I am if any hon. member wishes to ask them.
The hon. member also rather deplored the fact that the federal government was not spending more money in the field of highways. He referred to the large revenues the federal government is collecting from automobiles on the one hand and the relatively small expenditures we are making on highways on the other. There again I simply wish to remind him that the $20 million shown in the particular item to which he referred is not by any means the total of federal government expenditure on highways in this country. We are entirely responsible for all roads in national parks, for example, which is quite an item of expenditure. We are entirely responsible for highways in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon, with the cooperation of the government there, and that normally involves a high level of expenditure. The federal government is solely responsible for the maintenance of the Alaska highway, which is another expensive example. All these things add up to considerably more money than the amount to which my hon. friend referred.
Then he mentioned the temporary buildings in Ottawa. May I interrupt my remarks, Mr. Chairman, to say how glad 1 am to see the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in his place.
Thank you.

To revert to the question of temporary buildings in Ottawa, I think we all share the hon. member's desire that they be removed at as early a date as possible. Number 1 temporary building is scheduled to go just as soon as the trade and commerce building can be completed. We want the site of No. 1 temporary building on which to build the national library, and we hope that can be undertaken next year. Just as soon as accommodation can be provided to move other people out of their temporary quarters the temporary accommodation will be torn down, and that cannot come too quickly as far as 1 am concerned.

Supply-Public Works
The hon. member referred to the fact that we are now spending more of our votes than previously. That is true. In the past fiscal year we would have had quite a good record if we had been able to hold the position that we attained in the first three-quarters of the fiscal year. However, toward the latter part we were held up by shortages of materials, and for that reason we were not able to spend as much money as we otherwise would have spent.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni spoke about the dilemma in which he feels I find myself in trying to run the Department of Public Works. This is the first time it has crossed my mind that I was confronted with a dilemma. I feel that for some reason or other he believes that the Minister of Finance has imposed a limitation on the operations of the Department of Public Works, and that is creating difficulties for us. The fact of the matter is that when we were contemplating our estimates for this year we in the department took the view that the role of the Department of Public Works should certainly not be to go into the field and compete with private investment for money, materials or manpower if by so doing we would operate to the detriment of the general growth and development of Canada.
After all, our job is to provide services for Canada, and if Canada does not develop as it should we will not have the same need subsequently to provide services to the extent we would like. I think it is our job to aid and abet the development of Canada, and if by slowing down our program and giving private developers a freer hand it could be done more expeditiously, then I believe that is our role. I think we in the department are growing with Canada. I believe the best evidence of that is that in 1945 the total vote for this department was $23 million, of which $19 million was spent. The following year, 1946, the first full year after the war, the total was $29 million, of which $22 million was spent. Against that we place the amount shown in the estimates before the committee now, which is a total of $167,865,940.
The hon. member for New Westminster spoke of certain difficulties which he thought we were encountering. I assure him I see none of those difficulties. I feel we have a good staff in the department now; we have a good program, and we are operating within the framework of good government policy. I think whatever difficulties the hon. member may think he sees ahead of us can be readily overcome. The other questions raised were on particular items and perhaps we could leave them.
I can say to my hon. friend from Calgary North, who expressed some concern about


the building program in Calgary, that I too have been disappointed that we have not been able to get on with our program there. We have had difficulties of various kinds, including indecision amongst the different departments as to what accommodation was required and difficulties about the acquisition of a site. However, I believe that progress is now being made. We have selected a firm of architects and they are in the preliminary stages of developing plans. If we are able to iron out the difficulties that still obtain with respect to a site we have in mind, I would think we could start construction of a building next year. The reason there is nothing in the estimates now is that, as hon. members know, it is present policy of the department not to carry votes in the estimates unless there is a reasonable prospect that we will be able to put the work in hand during that particular fiscal year. It did not seem we could get on with the job this year so we dropped the vote, but that does not mean we have dropped the project.
Then a question was raised about these very serious fire losses, particularly in houses in the Ottawa area where I understand some 50 lives were lost during the past winter. It is doubtless true that some of the fires and some of the losses resulted from faulty wiring. Having that in mind, a question arises as to what should be done about it and who should do it. As both the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Prince Albert said, this is a matter that clearly falls within the jurisdiction of provincial and municipal governments. Through the agency of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, who administer the National Housing Act, we can and do lay down certain standards for wiring and other particulars of construction. I think hon. members are aware that fire losses in houses built under the National Housing Act have been relatively minor. I do not know of any case in which lives have been lost in a building constructed under the statute.
We have endeavoured to create an awareness of this hazard. Officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Department of Public Works, are working with the national research council, which is endeavouring to disseminate research knowledge and consciousness of this problem to all the municipalities. Our own dominion fire commissioner has been in touch with all the provincial fire marshals across Canada and later this year, in September I believe, there is to be a meeting on the west coast which will be attended by the deputy minister of public works. There will then be a full and

I hope fruitful discussion of this whole problem with a view to trying at least to create sufficient awareness of this very real hazard to reduce these very serious losses of life.
The hon. member for Huron asked about the building at Exeter, and I can tell him that tenders have been called. I would think before too long we would be able to award a contract for the additions and alterations there. The hon. member for Prince Albert raised questions about two large buildings in the Ottawa area, the printing bureau and the dominion bureau of statistics. The printing bureau is undoubtedly an expensive structure. It is a very large building and I think it is a good building. I believe when it is completed and fully occupied the hon. member will come to the conclusion that there is good utilization of space there. I think the site is good having regard to the purposes for which the building is used. I do not believe it has all the disadvantages which were attributed to it this morning by the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario.
In so far as the construction of the bureau of statistics is concerned, I can well appreciate that the hon. member for Prince Albert would raise a question as to why it has been necessary to undertake large expenditures on a building so recently completed. I raised the same questions he did. We had-when I say "we" it was before my time, but that does not remove the responsibility from me-that building designed by a competent firm of architects. It was built by a competent contractor. When you ask me just where the responsibility lies for the conditions which have required us to undertake additional expenditures, I am not in a position to pinpoint it. The deputy minister informs me we have had meetings and tried to assess the responsibility.
There is no doubt about it; we have learned lessons from this. There were certain defects arising from the windows, and they contributed to the uneven heating in the wintertime. I think the same condition contributed to some of the problems encountered in the summertime. The hon. member asked if we have learned anything from these conditions, and the answer is yes. I hope they will not be repeated. We have not had many instances where new buildings have required such extensive repairs. I will certainly do my best to see that it does not happen again.

May I ask the minister, was an endeavour made by the officials of the department or by any outside body to ascertain the reason for these defects that were found to exist in the statistics building?
Supply-Public Works
Yes, that was done, Mr. Chairman. The deputy minister had a series of meetings with the contractor and the architects, as well as officials of our own department.

Has the minister a copy of the report that was made? I understand there were two reports made in connection with the examples of the inefficiency-I hesitate to use the word, but I think that is the only word I can use-revealed by the examination that was made. Is it not a fact that there are two reports? If so, will the minister table those reports?

The only reports that have come to my attention, Mr. Chairman, are departmental reports from the deputy minister to me, or from one of the officials to the deputy minister; and those reports are, of course, privileged documents. If there is any other report that comes to my attention I shall be pleased to discuss it with the hon. member to see whether or not he would wish it to be tabled.
Mr. Chairman, I presume we are still on the first item. Is that so?

speechtext: Yes.

I am sorry I was not in the house to hear the complete speech made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I presume he dealt with what is more or less a joint problem of the riding of Okanagan-Revelstoke and his own riding. I am sure from conversations we have had that he was dealing in some way with the question of dredging in the Arrow lake where the Columbia enters that lake. I believe the lake is his responsibility, and the town of Arrowhead and the land on the north is in my riding. I have a file from the board of trade in Arrowhead containing some correspondence they had with this department over the particular problem in that area.
I have talked this over with the hon. member for Kootenay West, and we have come to the conclusion that some dredging in the lake would widen the channel for the incoming water from the Columbia and eliminate the spreading action which it has at the present time. It is this narrowness of depth and the width to which it spreads that is the source of a lot of trouble in causing ice-jamming and ice-packing at the mouth of the river. According to advice from the board of trade at Arrowhead, I understand there has been some damage to the wharf there so far this winter, and further damage is expected this spring. We do believe that is the responsibility of the Department of Public Works, and we think it should be-and I feel sure it will be-attended to.
2922	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
But the matter of erosion is just a little bit bigger problem. We understand that 35 feet of soil from the bank of the Columbia along the railway right of way into the town has already disappeared, and the whole question of erosion is quite serious. It is causing a lot of trouble to pole operators and sawmills. We took this up with the department. I have a very pleasant letter, ending with the regrets of the deputy minister that they could not see their way clear to spend as much money as their engineers had estimated it would cost to remedy the situation.
I am satisfied that the board of trade-and I know this from my own thinking-would not be justified in asking for the huge expenditure that would be required to take care of this matter. It would cost upwards of $500,000. I am satisfied that the people of that area are not expecting such a retaining wall, although as a permanent solution something along those lines may have to be studied and adopted. At the same time we are asking and hoping that the channel in the lake will be dredged and deepened to prevent this flooding by the river as it enters into the lake, which would eliminate or decrease the piling and jamming of ice and the erosion that takes place. Temporary measures will have to be taken.
I understand that the provincial department of agriculture set up some machinery during the last session of the legislature to make a study of river erosion in British Columbia. It is just in its initial stages, but I am satisfied that if or when this new department has been set up and is in operation in our province they will be prepared to co-operate fully with the federal department in seeking a solution to some of the problems.
While we have this letter refusing to spend the large amount of money which their engineers have claimed would be necessary, I should like to assure the minister that we are not asking for or expecting such a huge sum, but we do request that the whole question be looked at again and that the engineer get down to business with the people concerned there to see if some temporary and less expensive solution cannot be found to their problem. It is not only in Arrowhead. The Columbia river flows through the entire Revelstoke area, and there is a problem along its entire length. The whole thing will eventually have to be studied and some solution will have to be found to the problem of erosion. For the present we would request that immediate action be taken to find a solution to the problem that is facing the people in the Arrowhead district.
tMr. McLeod.]

Mr. Chairman, I am very happy this afternoon to hear so many worthy compliments paid to the Minister of Public Works, the deputy minister and his department. No doubt they worked well as a team in the last war, and they are working well as a team now. I hope later on to be able to say that I am as satisfied in Bruce as several hon. members have been able to say here this afternoon.
There are several projects in Bruce that we are vitally interested in. The reason I rise at this time is that a project I have in mind has not been included in the estimates that have been tabled. It concerns a proposed post office in Teeswater. I had a question on the order paper on February 17 of this year, and the answers I received were very satisfactory. What I would like to get across to the minister is this. I would ask him to bring down the supplementary estimate as soon as possible to permit the building to get started in Teeswater so it can be finished in 1956, as the answers to my question indicated.
That is the only point I wish to make at this time. I can discuss the other problems we have when the details of the estimates are before the committee.

I want to take just a moment or two on this particular item, Mr. Chairman. I want to express the appreciation that the people from our area would want me to express to the department and its officials for the work it is doing in Qu'Appelle. We have no large cities; we have just small towns in our particular area, but through the years the services that have been rendered by government departments have grown. For example, a little post office which had perhaps a turnover of $300 in 1910 has a turnover today of $10,000; consequently the locations of the post offices have become woefully inadequate in many instances.
I wish to say that the department is cooperating in a splendid way in helping to meet the wishes of the people for better service accommodation. I should say, too, that in a small locality like ours where improved services are required, a local interest exists as to what type of building shall house the services. The department and its officials have been most co-operative in discussing local problems with the local boards of trade and interested citizens.
I might give an example of that. When the plans first came out for the new building to house the R.C.M.P. at Broadview, some people felt they were not in line with local thinking. Certain suggestions were made concerning minor but fairly important changes. We

were very happy that some changes were made at the request of local people. We have found the officials extremely co-operative in trying to meet the wishes of the people in the local community.
The minister has also been extremely cooperative. It was my privilege during the Easter recess to open a new public building at Kipling, the youngest town in Saskatchewan, and a beautiful little structure it is, indeed. It is not out of line with the size of the place. At first there were ambitious plans advanced by the local community calling for a much larger building. The department cooperated and we all got together and worked out the problems. While the cost of the present building is only a fraction of the original figure that was kicked around, if I may express it in those terms, the local citizens are very satisfied.
At the time of this opening the roads and highways were blocked, and there were walls of snow ten feet high. It was snowing and sleeting that afternoon. Despite the bad weather 400 people from neighbouring towns, including reeves, councillors and mayors, attended the opening. It was really a great tribute to the co-operative spirit which existed between the local community and the Department of Public Works.
I must say I was highly impressed by the officials who attended. They gave us every assistance in making the opening a worthwhile effort. I want to thank the minister for inviting me to officiate on his behalf on that occasion. The people in that area certainly appreciate the attention and the apparent interest shown by the department in serving that community.
Let me repeat that while we do hear certain criticisms of the department here and there, that sort of thing is bound to occur in any government undertaking. It seems that everyone has a licence to criticize the government in what it does. You always get a great many local, self-appointed experts who are convinced in some instances that they know more than the architect and the minister. In the main, however, we have experienced great co-operation from the Department of Public Works in my constituency.
I want to again express to the minister the great appreciation we have for his interest in our particular area. The minister and his department appear to realize that in our development through the years we have outgrown our existing accommodation. Our area dates in history from the 1870's. As I said at the beginning of my remarks there is a need for public buildings of the kind we are now getting.
Supply-Public Works
I wish to thank the minister once more for inviting me to officiate at the opening of the new building to which I have referred, and to again express the appreciation of this and other communities in Qu'Appelle for what is being done in that area.
Mr. Chairman, I have just one matter to place before the minister. Does the Department of Public Works have any responsibility whatever in connection with the removal of Ripple Rock?
Yes, that comes under the jurisdiction of public works.

Could the minister explain to the committee the progress that has been made with that work? I cannot find any vote in the minister's estimates to cover it, and I am just wondering what provision is made for it?

Has the Department of Public Works sole jurisdiction over this work or is any other department concerned?

Perhaps when the vote comes up the minister could give the house a statement as to what progress has been made and when it is expected the rock will be removed.

361. British Columbia. $6,495,000.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about this item. I should like to expand upon one or two suggestions I made earlier, and perhaps particularize some of my remarks of this morning. I said I felt that generally the progress made in supplying public buildings and other services has not been geared to the expansion of our economy.
In this connection I would refer specifically to the northern part of Vancouver island, which is one area in Canada which is growing with extreme rapidity. I mentioned that in the Alberni valley there are one or two areas where extensive developments in the pulp and wood products industries are taking place. I know the department has some property in Port Alberni for a new public building, but I felt I should raise this item specifically and suggest to the minister that in view of the rapid growth that is taking place, any plans the department may have developed should be expedited and accelerated to the point where at least in some measure they keep pace with the industrial growth of the area.
In the Alberni valley there are two cities, Port Alberni and Alberni. In both cities there exists an acute shortage of space, particularly in the way of post office accommodation. I mentioned this morning that the present post office building in Port Alberni was erected in 1913. I might say at this point that it is not now able to meet the needs of the Post Office Department, let alone those of other branches of the federal government.
There is a nice little post office building in Alberni which, if I remember rightly, was erected about 1938 or 1939, but here again the facilities available are not sufficient to meet the needs of the present population. The whole situation has been affected by the rapid growth that is taking place. If plans are being considered for the provision of


accommodation in this area I hope they will be accelerated in order to meet the present need.
While I am dealing with this subject I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the almost phenomenal growth which has taken place in Campbell River. I know the department has plans for a federal building in this centre which has developed from a small tourist, fishing and logging village into one of the major industrial centres on Vancouver island. Here again I would urge that if plans are being formulated, they be accelerated in order that the department may give attention to this particular project.
Those are the two points in my district where I feel that the time lag to which I referred earlier is most acute. I should like to emphasize the importance of a program for the provision of public buildings in these two areas.

Mr. Chairman, during the past year a building which was being used by officials administering the Veterans' Land Act was vacated and I understand that these officials were moved to the public building in New Westminster. A new addition to this building is now under construction. Could the minister indicate the circumstances under which these officials were moved, whether it was the policy of the government to have them moved into the building to which they were moved, or just why this was done? The lease on the building in which they had been accommodated was up for renewal. Were there any other circumstances having to do with their leaving the building?
As far as I know it was just a routine move. I do not know of any unusual circumstances.

Would the minister care to enlarge on my other question with respect to the development of the public building in New Westminster? As 1 understand it the present plans call for a portion to be built at this time and the demolition of the present post office, which will be rebuilt. Just what are the plans with respect to that building?
I shall get a report on that for my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, I understand you are taking these items province by province and have slipped by Nova Scotia, but I just want to ask the minister one question. About two months ago I noticed an announcement in the press, apparently by the official project announcer, that there were plans under consideration for a new public building in Glace Bay, presumably to replace the present post office. Could the minister state whether any official consideration has been given to that

particular project, or was that announcement just the result of somebody's imagination?
What was the nature of the announcement?
That there was to be a new public building in Glace Bay replacing the present post office. This would be quite a big project.

I should like to see the announcement to which my hon. friend refers. We have nothing of a definite nature. We have been giving some thought to accommodation in Glace Bay, but we have not advanced to the stage where there is anything definite.
Still under consideration.

While we are on this particular item I should like to call the minister's attention to the need for a federal building in the village of Hope, British Columbia. We hope it will become a reality. This matter was called to the attention of the postal department some time ago. It was brought to my attention first by a letter from the municipal clerk of the corporation of the village of Hope, dated July 31, 1954. The letter states:
Dear Sir:
The Hope village commissioners have instructed me to place before you the matter of a federal *building in Hope, in the near future.
The post office has been rather inadequately housed for years in various rented premises, and is about to be moved again.
The commissioners feel that with Hope's growth the last few years, consideration might be given to a government building. They would like to ask your opinion on this, and your assistance.
Yours truly,
M. G. H. Stuart,
Municipal Clerk.
Upon receipt of that letter, I communicated with the Postmaster General, the late Hon. Alcide Cote, and called this matter to his attention, pointing out that Hope was a very progressive town in the Fraser valley, having shown substantial growth throughout the past number of years, and at the present time has a population of approximately 3,000. New industries are in prospect for this area, and with these additional developments the area certainly will continue to grow at a very rapid rate. In reply 1 was advised that the Postmaster General could not recommend the erection of a building at that particular time because of the fact that arrangements had been made for rented premises, which they found were adequate for the present.
However, I should like to point out again today that Hope is a very progressive community. Certainly I feel that some definite consideration should be given to the erection
Supply-Public Works of a federal building in this locality. At the present time Hope is in need of further government services. Of course, as 1 have indicated, it is in need of additional postal facilities. The present facilities are now not sufficient to take care of the situation.
There is also need for a national employment service office, and this was brought to my attention in the past few weeks. At the present time the persons concerned have to travel a considerable distance to get to the nearest office, which causes considerable delay and inconvenience and entails considerable expense on the part of those who have to make a considerable number of trips to Chilliwack. Such a building could house this particular office and also a veterans affairs office, the closest one being located also at Chilliwack.
There is also the suggestion that they could possibly have a fisheries office there. I understand that previously one was located at Hope but it had been closed. At the present time the meteorological office is housed in very small rented premises in the village of Hope. Therefore I suggest that these conditions warrant the erection of a federal building. On behalf of the people of that community I would ask the minister and the government to give consideration to this matter, with a view to bringing in something along those lines, at least by the time the next estimates are introduced in the house.

I should like to answer a question asked by the hon. member for New Westminster about the building there. The contract that is under way now is for the construction of the first portion of the work, that is, the building of a portion of the whole project which is on the property we acquired from the city. When that is finished the occupants of the present portion of the building will move into the new building, and the old building will be renovated.

I have long waited for this item of the estimates to come before this house. I was very pleased last fall to receive from the department an invitation to attend the laying of the cornerstone of the new so-called $10 million post office in the city of Vancouver. I notice that the city of New Westminster is also getting a new public building. I am not going to criticize that. I think these progressive cities of British Columbia are well worth the investing of substantial sums of money.
However, I should like to call to the minister's attention that this house some time ago had a debate, rather limited because of the application of the rules of this house, in which by means of a resolution we were asking the federal government to take advantage of

Supply-Public Works every possible opportunity to promote the decentralization of industry. I should like to submit to the minister that the business of the federal government is the greatest business that now exists in the Dominion of Canada. Before this government attempts too strongly to advise industry to decentralize, it should do some decentralizing of its own enterprises throughout the country.
What I have reference to is the tendency to consolidate and establish huge centralized sections of various departments of government in some of the major cities. I could speak for hours on the subject of the evil effects such a policy will have. However, I am going to limit myself to making only a few remarks on it.
Whilst I am glad that a city the size of New Westminster, with a population of some 30,000, is getting a new public building, I should like to ask the minister when the 78,000 people in Burnaby will be considered a large enough population to deserve a public building. It has been asked for on a number of occasions. Just before the 1953 election there was an item in the estimates for that purpose. I do not know whether or not that was only to enable the Liberal candidate to win re-election to this house. However, since the election it is to be noted that that item has disappeared from the estimates, and I would very much like the minister to give us a little information on what progress, if any, is being made. I do not complain at all-

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman has created some suspicion in this house that an amount was put in the public works estimates to allow me to be re-elected in Burnaby-Richmond. I hope he will assure the house that the impression I got was not correct.

I noted the hon. member entering the house while I was speaking. I do not think he followed my argument completely. I was asking the minister for information as to why this item for a public building for Burnaby was in the estimates in that election year and has since been taken out of the estimates. It has not been revoted, and I have seen little headway being made since that time in putting up a public building in Burnaby.
I know the minister takes the attitude that he will not put up a public building unless he is asked to do so by some particular minister on behalf of some particular department of government. In other words, if the Postmaster General would ask him to put up a public building in Burnaby he would do so. However, I feel he should also know the utter IMr. Begier.]
chaos that has existed for several years now in the Post Office Department, and the Postmaster General is not yet well enough acclimatized to his new responsibilities to know whether or not a place such as Burnaby is actually in need of a post office building.
The people there resent the discrimination. They do not like all these things centred in the major cities surrounding them. I know that public buildings have been erected in some relatively minor places. I believe White Rock and Cloverdale have new public buildings. I noted that the hon. member for Fraser Valley put in a plea for a public building at Hope. In addition to the 78,000 people in Burnaby who want a federal public building erected, there are also some 4,000 people in the city of Port Moody who are in need of a public building. Recently the people of Port Coquitlam put forth considerable effort to get a public building. The city council there, with the support of various ratepayer organizations and the board of trade, asked for the erection of a public building to accommodate not only the post office but other departments of government as well.
They feel that these departments should be decentralized. There is not much personal contact between unemployed men and the officer placing men in employment if the men are lined up for several blocks before they reach the official. We believe that if more unemployment offices were set up throughout the country more efficient service would be rendered to the unemployed, because the officers in smaller offices would be in much closer touch with the needs of employers in the area and would have a much more personal knowledge of the particular occupations that the unemployed would be able to fill.
I have not done so before, but at this time I should like to make a plea to the minister to consider seriously the problem of when is the time to award public buildings to rapidly growing suburban areas in the fast developing regions of Canada. I have attempted to find out from various officials in the minister's department exactly what are the conditions under which a public building will be agreed to by the department. I find there is no set or fixed rule. Each case is decided on its own merits, and when you attempt to find out what the merits are that warrant a public building you run up against a wall. You cannot find out. You think maybe if there is a Liberal member for the district that will help bring about the erection of a public building.
I can assure the minister that I found that was not the case even before he became minister. The people of my riding elected a Liberal member in the year 1940 and then

re-elected him in 1945. He is now Minister of Fisheries. In 1949 they elected the hon. gentleman who is now the member for Burnaby-Richmond in what used to be his riding. Yet after all these years the needs of the people have not been met. Therefore it is obvious that party patronage is not the deciding factor, and I should like to compliment the department on that fact. The people back home felt that electing a Liberal for all those years did not get them a public building, so why should they not vote for something else for a change.
I hope the minister can give us some indication of exactly what is the deciding factor with respect to when a community can obtain a public building. Is it only on the basis of a request from some other department of government, or are there any other factors that I have not yet been able to discover? When places like White Rock and Cloverdale are provided with public buildings, when I hear a plea made for a public building for a relatively small city such as Hope-and I am sure the hon. member for Fraser Valley feels keenly that Hope should have a public building-I should like to know under what conditions some 78,000 people can expect to obtain a public building.

I should like to revert briefly to item 353 in order to take this opportunity to ask the minister to report briefly on the progress made in the construction of the federal building in Charlottetown and when it is expected it will be ready for occupation.
At the end of March 81 per cent of the building had been completed and paid for. The target date for completion is September 27, 1956.
Could I ask the minister about the item of $100,000 for Saint John? I presume that is for the new customs building. Would the minister say what progress is being made?

I can only tell my hon. friend that the plans for the building are proceeding very well. We have an estimated date by which we hope to be able to call for tenders. That is around the latter part of this year. I have November of this year as the target date. I would not want the hon. member to feel I was binding myself to that date because there are too many variables between now and then, but we are hoping to go to tender somewhere around the end of the present year.

I appreciate the statement of the minister and I should like to express my thoughts with respect to the replacement of
Supply-Public Works the old building. I used all the adjectives I could use in the last two years but once again I urge all haste in replacing the old building. During the Easter holidays I took my life in my hands and walked around the old building in Saint John. While half of it is roped off, it is a danger and an eyesore to the whole community. One of the gentlemen there at the time pointed out to me a piece of the ledge that had fallen off the building and had just missed the arm of the collector of customs by two or three feet. Therefore it is not only an eyesore but we may be losing valuable civil servants if something is not done.

I hesitate to enter the debate twice in one day, but I think an explanation is due the house with regard to the amount of $75,000, of which the present minister knows nothing. That was done under the former minister, and I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam should be straightened out on the matter. He is quite right in saying that $75,000 was put in the estimates. That was the amount arranged to purchase certain properties in the southern part of Burnaby close to his present boundary, and the money was to be spent to buy the land for a federal building. As soon as these people found out that the federal government was going to purchase the property the price went up overnight to $160,000. I suggested to the minister at that time that the purchase not be made and the amount was taken out of the estimates.

I should like to ask the minister two questions under this item, which I understand has to do with British Columbia public buildings. Can he inform the house when he expects the public building at Trail to be completed, and also the public building at Castlegar?
The target date for the completion of the building at Trail is March of 1957. The target date for the completion of the building at Castlegar is in August of this year.

Yes. I should like to thank the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond for the information he has given this committee. I still have not had an answer from the minister, and I should like to point out to him we now have a new city hall in a central location in Burnaby and it is a very beautiful

Supply-Public Works building. I should like to ask him if there is any hope of his department purchasing a site in that vicinity within the foreseeable future. Unless he takes action soon he is apt to find that he will be paying many, many times the amount of money for which that site for a future public building could be purchased today. He knows Burnaby and knows there are 75,000 to 80,000 people there now and will be 125,000 before many years have gone by. I share the consternation of my hon. friend when he says he does not understand why we are not receiving recognition. I understand that the Post Office Department will have to requisition this building. We want two offices in the building, one for war veterans allowances and one for unemployment insurance. My hon. friend and I are going to keep calling for this until we get an appropriation in the estimates.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Can the minister tell us when he expects the new Winnipeg post office building to be completed? My second question is, can the minister assure us there will not be an interruption in employment on this building next winter as there was this past winter?

The chances are, Mr. Chairman, that the building will be completed before we get fully through another winter construction season. But if that is not the case, then I should like to feel that I can assure my hon. friend there will be no interruptions. I think he knows to what extremes we went to avoid interruption there during this past winter season. In answer to his specific question, we feel that the building will be fully completed and ready for occupancy by February of next year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Perhaps the minister might take one more question which arises out of that answer. Has any decision yet been made as to what the government intends to do with the old post office building on Portage avenue?

A final decision has not been made, Mr. Chairman, but we think it will be declared surplus and turned over to the crown assets corporation.
364. Unforeseen improvements, $900,000.

The particulars in connection with this item are given at page 469 of the estimates, and I notice that last year there was a vote of $1 million but the actual expenditure, together with an estimate for the last three months, totalled $350,000. Why is it necessary to put in a figure of $900,000 this year? [DOT] It would seem that there is some excess in that. As I understand it, this is a general item to cover improvements that are not foreseen at the moment. It would appear that this figure of $900,000, even though it is $100,000 less than last year, is in excess of what is required.

Mr. Chairman, I am told we borrowed against that vote from time to time considerably in excess of the $350,000 shown. The vote was very useful in that way. I do not know whether $900,000 will be too much this year. It is a matter of contingencies, and I can assure my hon. friend it has been very useful on occasions.
Then the figure of $900,000 in this vote is, in effect, a fictitious figure? The vote is used by the department for borrowing money for some other purpose entirely?

It is a matter of protection against unforeseen events, such as storm damage and things of that nature. It is an estimate of what we might require. There is no way of determining with any precision just what will be required. I hope we do not need any of it.
It is past five o'clock anyway, so perhaps the minister could look into that further and let us have a more detailed statement when the estimates are again under discussion.

I do not know what more I can give, but if there is anything more I will give it.
Item stands'.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Richardson for the second reading of Bill No. 166, to incorporate the Signature Loan and Finance Company, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ellis.

Mr. Speaker, it is nearly three weeks now since I was interrupted in the middle of a sentence by the winged chariot of time, and since I have an aversion to leaving sentences hanging in mid air I would like, with your permission, to finish that sentence.
On looking up Hansard of March 27 I see that I was dealing with a suggestion offered by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Carrick) that the objections that were being made to this particular measure were of a type that could be equally well made against such an investment as that in the Aluminum Company of Canada, and I was suggesting that such an analogy was completely false and completely misleading.
Now you may say, sir, that the objections to this bill have been based on the ground that it is a foreign company; but I submit to you the fact that it is a foreign company is merely an aggravation of the situation with which we disagree. To draw an analogy between a foreign investment such as that made by a company like the Aluminum Company, which comes into the productive enterprise of this country and increases the wealth production of the country, and an organization such as is envisaged in this bill, which is coming here merely, as I said earlier, to batten on the misfortunes of the Canadian people, is I think a very misleading thing to do.
Private Bills
I do not think it makes a great deal of difference, sir, whether it is Canadian racketeers or foreign racketeers who get into this particular business, but I do think this house should give serious consideration to the evident state of affairs in this country which provides a happy hunting ground for just such organizations as this, whether they be foreign or native. And rather than providing an opportunity for another organization to profit by the misfortunes of the Canadian people, we should be examining very carefully our responsibilities toward the Canadian people to see why it is there are apparently a growing number of our fellow citizens who are obliged at one time or another to take advantage of the lending facilities of those companies, even at the outrageous interest rates they charge. I suggest, sir, the very fact that those companies are able to operate and find customers within the Canadian community for loans at interest rates of 23 per cent and 24 per cent per annum indicates very clearly that there is something radically wrong in our economy.
It is not so very many years ago, sir, when it was commonly accepted that it was a very serious state of affairs for people to get into the hands of moneylenders. Various pieces of legislation were introduced to attempt to control that situation, and lending institutions had their powers to set interest rates very greatly curbed. But I suggest to you, sir, that the ability of companies still to charge 23 per cent and 24 per cent indicates that we have not gone nearly far enough. I would therefore support wholeheartedly the motion of my colleague from Regina City (Mr. Ellis) that this bill be given the six months' hoist.
Furthermore, I would suggest that the government take a very serious look at the situation in Canada which is apparently enticing those corporations to come into our country to batten, as I say, on the misfortunes of Canadian citizens. It is merely an aggravation that this is a purely foreign company coming here, not, incidentally, to lend foreign funds to Canadian citizens but, if it follows the practice of existing companies in this field, to borrow Canadian money from Canadian banks to lend to Canadian citizens, and to take the profits from those transactions outside this country. Therefore, sir, I support this six months' hoist and very seriously recommend it to hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, this bill, together with another very similar bill has been discussed by my colleagues on a number of occasions now. I think they are to be commended for bringing this matter forcibly to the attention of the Canadian public. We are not so naive as to think we can outvote the supporters of the government

Private Bills
if they are inclined to support this bill or any other bill in the house, but we have a duty and a privilege to bring to the attention of the public any legislation we feel is tending toward dangerous ground. The number of bills that have appeared this session dealing with finance companies and lending institutions generally, including legislation proposed by the government itself dealing with lending, is really amazing. One begins to wonder just what the end is going to be.
This particular bill is an attempt to incorporate a new finance company. It is interesting in several respects, but to me it is most interesting because of the appearance again as one of the directors of a gentleman by the name of Duncan Kenneth MacTavish. I want it clearly understood sir, that anything I have to say about this gentleman is not meant to be derogatory or critical of him as a person. I have no personal knowledge of this gentleman whatever. All I know is of his connections.
On looking through the various finance bills that have appeared here, and the small loans companies generally, I find that this gentleman appears with monotonous regularity as a director of those companies. One begins to wonder how he has attained this great ubiquity in the finance world in Canada. If one links that up with the fact that he is the president of the national Liberal federation, then one has reason to wonder whether, in addition to the attempt that has been made by various Liberal leaders in this country recently to establish a one-party system in politics, they are not trying to extend that into the economic field.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is that not awful?
I heard someone across the way say, "nonsense".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I said, "Is that not awful?"

I beg your pardon; I thought I heard the word "nonsense". Of course we are so used to hearing "nonsense" from across the way that I was leading up to a reply to it.
There is a danger, a very definite danger, when the president of a political party of nation-wide importance finds himself director, chairman, vice-president, and so forth, of a great plethora of financial institutions in this country. Without saying anything derogatory about this gentleman himself, as I said, I think we should know, this house should know and the country should know, what some of his financial connections are.
I have before me an excerpt taken from the Financial Post. This was in 1955, and may not be right up to date. If he has in the

meantime divested himself of any of these positions, of course that will have to be taken as understood. However, according to this report, Mr. MacTavish is quoted as being connected with the following firms: chairman of the Jubilee Brewery Company.
We have heard that.

Someone across the way says, "We have heard that". I am putting this on the record because, as a matter of fact, when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) stated some of the business connections of this gentleman, he did not mention the ones I am now mentioning. This is in addition to the list which is already on the record. He is chairman of the Jubilee Brewery Company; president of Bestec (Canada) Limited; president of CKOY Limited; president of W. D. Morris Realty Limited; president of Primco Limited; vicepresident and director of the Holden Manufacturing Company Limited; of Instruments Limited and of the Metcalfe Realty Company Limited; secretary and director of Pitney-Bowes of Canada Limited; member of the executive committee and director of the Southam Company of Canada Limited; director of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, the Crown Life Insurance Company, Gatineau Power Company, Ottawa Car and Aircraft Limited, Associated Screen News Limited, and New York Capital Fund of Canada Limited. That is really a good one; New York Capital Fund of Canada Limited. I would like an explanation of that.
He is also a director of Personal Finance Company of Canada, which now seeks to transform itself into the 'Beneficial Finance Company. He is a director, too, of Quality Records Limited, Textile Improvements Limited, Triarch Corporation Limited, British American Bank Note Company Limited, R. L. Crain Limited, Holt Renfrew and Company Limited, Sylvania Electric (Canada) Limited and the Royal Trust Company.
That is a very impressive list of firms with which to be connected. One begins to wonder why it is that this same gentleman is asked to appear as director, chairman or vice-president, etc., of all these different companies. Surely it is not simply because he is capable and efficient. Regardless of how capable and efficient he may be it is not because he could give his personal attention to the direction, in a business sense, of all these different companies with which he is connected; that, of course, would be physically impossible. It makes one wonder whether or not an attempt is being made by means of these interlocking directorships to have a friend in court, to have a gentleman

available who happens to be president of the national Liberal federation of Canada as a sort of insurance.
One can well imagine how very convenient such an arrangement might be. Let us take the operation of the average finance company. What do they need? First of all, of course, they need money, so Mr. MacTavish, as director, can go to the Canadian Bank of Commerce or he can go to the New York Capital Fund of Canada Limited, the Royal Trust Company or the Crown Life Insurance Company in order to ask for funds.
Another thing these companies require and which it seems to me they use to an excessive extent is publicity and advertising. Mr. MacTavish therefore finds himself a director of the Southam Press; very convenient. He is also a director of Associated Screen News Limited.
Perhaps finance companies require good business locations, the most advantageous locations in a city. Mr. MacTavish also happens to be vice-president and director of the Metcalfe Realty Company; also very convenient.
Perhaps at times they might even wish to provide a little music and light entertainment, possibly at the time the national Liberal federation is having a convention in the city of Ottawa. Well, Mr. MacTavish is vice-president and director of Instruments Limited. I suppose that would be very convenient, too. When it comes to refreshments it is perhaps most convenient of all, because Mr. MacTavish is chairman of Jubilee Breweries. He is also a director of Quality Records Limited. In view of this arrangement I think it might be appropriate if the Liberal party were to have a theme song. It might well be the "Beer Barrel Polka", because recent developments indicate that brewery companies are rather closely connected, finance-wise, with the Liberal party in the province of Ontario, and I have no doubt that the same obtains right across Canada.
These are some of the considerations of importance. I think the Canadian public will be well advised to heed the advice that has been given in this house by several of my colleagues, and particularly in an excellent speech given the other day by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett)-
We will be really hard up when we have to go to you fellows for advice.

-when he drew attention to the excellent service that can be provided in the small loans field by the credit union movement in Canada. I think if this government wanted to do something really constructive and useful in the way of providing
Private Bills
cash to people at a reasonable cost it would do something to promote the credit union movement by assisting it in providing the facilities and services it has available.
There is a world of difference between the way the credit union operates and the way these finance companies operate. We now have plenty of figures on record to indicate that even with a very small capitalization, and usually with foreign capital, the finance companies can come into our country, borrow money from the chartered banks and insurance companies with which they are interlocked in their directorships, and then use that money which they get at a low interest rate to lend out at interest rates running as high as 24 per cent. The profit goes back to the shareholders of the companies concerned. A great proportion of it goes back to the United States and performs no service to the Canadian people.
The credit union movement, on the other hand, because it belongs to the members of the society and because it is based on service to the community and is a non-profit organization which is designed to serve the community, operates in a totally different way. The money left in surplus is distributed amongst the people who make use of the facilities in the form of dividends, and by cutting down the final interest rate that keeps the money in the community and helps to build it up. It is the most efficient and human way in which to solve our financial problems.
I think this house would be well advised to turn down this bill and go forward with helping the credit unions develop their facilities for financing.

Mr. Speaker, although my colleagues have covered a great deal of ground in discussing this legislation there are still a few comments which I feel should be made.
First of all I would like to commend two of the hon. senators for the extremely constructive comments they made while this bill was before the other place. I refer to Senator Croll and Senator Horner. Senator Croll quite correctly drew attention to the fact that the taking over of the small loans field by large United States corporations presents a serious threat to our economy. I am sure all hon. members are agreed that you cannot improve economic conditions for the people in the lower income brackets by encouraging them to divert an increasingly larger percentage of their total income into interest payments to loan sharks. When people are so desperately in need of goods that they feel obliged to pay 26 per cent per annum in order to get the things which they cannot get with their limited resources, they are merely postponing an evil day.

The last annual report of the superintendent of insurance draws to our attention the control exercised by two major United States small loans companies now operating in Canada which do about 85 per cent of the business in this field. The remarkable growth of these two United States companies in the last four or five years is certainly alarming, and we now have another United States company coming into this field. It is indeed disturbing.
I find that this is an extremely profitable field as indicated in the superintendent's report. The small loans companies started out in 1950 with earned surpluses of $3-9 million, and these have gone up to $6-6 million. That is the net surplus, the cream they have been able to skim off the poor Canadians who feel obliged to go to their offices to get further and further into debt and pay interest at the rate of 26 per cent. This has enabled these companies who report to the superintendent to increase their net. The amount of capital stock has likewise increased during that period, and the total assets of these companies, owned and controlled 85 per cent by United States principals, were as follows:
1950		 $ 61,000,000
1951		 79,000,000
1952		 87,000,000
1953		 99,000,000
1954		 111,000,000
The last year for which returns are available is 1954. I submit that this alarming development which has been brought to our attention by the superintendent and also by Senator Croll should give us material for consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to a debate in the other place? If so, I am afraid I did not rise quickly enough to point out that he is not in order.

I merely mentioned that this matter did receive critical attention by two senators in the other place. When we consider conditions in the world today, where there are serious economic problems, where usury has developed, I think the extent to which it has developed in Canada poses a very real problem. I was interested In reading a speech delivered by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie) in 1949 after he had returned from a trip to China. He described most vividly the poverty he found in that country, and he said that while there he had obtained a much different outlook as to the purpose of Chiang Kai-shek who at that time was considered to be quite a hero. The hon. member pointed out that he had never seen poverty of that nature any place in the world in

which he had been. One reason for the upheaval in China was the fact that interest rates of 26 per cent had climbed to 46 and 50 per cent. When the poor people of any country find themselves in the position where they have to pay such fabulous interest charges it is a matter of national concern.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) referred to a memorandum which the Department of National Defence felt necessary to distribute to troops across the country in connection with this particular problem. The department pointed out that the Bank of Canada had reported that consumer credit had increased from $959 million in June, 1950, to $2,090 million in 1955. This was the total of charge and instalment accounts, loans, purchases of household goods, personal loans and small loans. Those who were responsible for the preparation of this memorandum had made a careful study of the situation and had observed the disturbing effect upon the morale of the troops because of problems that arose when members of the army, air force and navy found themselves in the clutches of these sharks, as they have been described by other hon. members who have spoken. It was pointed out quite accurately that people who were getting $200 a month should not get into debt so they have to pay an interest rate of 26 per cent in order to bridge the difference between what they are getting and what they think they would like to get.
Some of these companies making these fabulous profits have gone to a good deal of expense to insert advertisements in daily newspapers and periodicals which reflect upon the intelligence of hon. members of this house. They have made disparaging remarks about the credit union movement. While I was home at Easter I attended the annual meeting of the credit union of Sturgis. This organization has been kind enough to help me out from time to time when I have been in financial difficulties. The performance of this organization is considerably different from the performance of these large United States corporations which are fleecing poor Canadian people to the extent I have mentioned.
The credit union at Sturgis has been in operation since 1939. They now have a membership of 300. The members deposit their money with the local secretary when they are in funds, and then when credit problems arise the credit committee decides who are worthy to be granted loans. Since this credit union was established they have made loans totalling $414,924. They do not have to charge 26 per cent interest. As a matter of fact, not only do they make loans to their members, they provide insurance so that if the person obtaining a loan has the misfortune

to pass out of the picture before the loan is repaid the debt is written off. By using a small percentage of their net earnings they provide this insurance feature so the families who are left will not have to worry about discharging their debts.
I suggest that we would be better advised to be using some of our resources to encourage organizations of this type which are trying to combat the small loans companies. These companies spent a total of $1 million or more this year to try to convince people that they are their pals, that if they will only come to them they will be able to arrange trips to Florida and so on. Such advertising is misleading. One senator referred to this as being very much like the narcotic drug habit.
Order.

We should be concerned about granting further concessions to outside capital to come here and place our people in the position where they must pay 26 per cent interest in order to provide large dividends for men like the president of the national Liberal association and others who live south of the border. Therefore I hope that the six months' hoist which has been proposed by this group will have the support not only of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) who is absent today, but of all members on the other side. I would stress the fact that this is not a political matter, it is a matter of economics.

I shall vote against this amendment, and I think I had better say just a word as to why. This is a measure asking for the incorporation of a Company under well recognized practice. It is, I am advised, the invariable practice in these cases that these bills go to the banking and commerce committee, where the matter can be discussed. That seems to me to be in accordance with common sense and also in accordance with fairness.
We have been discussing this here in what appears to me a rather one-sided way, with no opportunity for the applicants to state their case. If the matter goes to the banking and commerce committee I think, as I said a moment ago, it will be in accordance with common sense and fairness, because there both sides will be represented. The applicants will be able to come and state their case. Those who are critical will be equally able to state their case. That seems to me as it should be.
In voting against this amendment I do not consider that I am voting in favour of the details of the bill. I consider myself entitled to discuss the matter when it comes before the banking and commerce committee, and
Private Bills
what I am voting for is to send the matter to the banking and commerce committee where, as I say, it can be discussed in what seems to me the proper manner.
Before I sit down I might point out that this matter has been before the other place, which followed the usual practice of allowing those who are making application for incorporation to state their case before the recognized parliamentary tribunal, shall I say, namely the banking and commerce committee.

I am very much disappointed to hear the statement by the hon. member for Greenwood as to the position the Conservative party is taking in this regard. I think it should be obvious to all members of this house and to all fair-minded Canadians that an interest rate that amounts to over 26 per cent a year is a disgrace to Canada, that it imposes a tremendous-	,

I rise on a point of order. My understanding is that we are discussing the incorporation of the company, and not at the present time the question of interest rates at all. That may very well come up. There is a bill in which it will come up, but I suggest that what we are discussing now, and the only thing we are discussing now, is a measure to refer the incorporation of this company to the banking and commerce committee.

Of course we are not discussing that either. We are discussing whether this bill should be given the six months' hoist, whether or not the bill should be killed. I am suggesting that the bill should be killed, because unless it is this company then will be given the same right that has now been given to other small loan companies, namely to charge an exorbitant and extortionate rate of interest of over 26 per cent a year.
Because we are thoroughly opposed to such a high and burdensome interest rate, and because we feel that this action will likely strengthen the institutions that are charging this exorbitant rate, we in this group have fought against this and other measures and hoped that we would convince members of this house that action should be taken to reduce the interest rates.
Surely we as members of parliament should not take the attitude that has been suggested, that we should give approval to the principle of the bill because that is the fair thing to do, because we can discuss the details in the banking and commerce committee and we can hear both sides, with the suggestion being made that the banking and commerce committee will give very fair and unbiased consideration to the representations

Private Bills
that will be made before it. We know from past experience that the committees of this house have a majority of government members on them.
Is that not proper?

I am not arguing against that. I am just stating it as a fact. The government has a majority of members on the committee. The government members almost never, if ever, oppose government policy-not Liberal members, anyway.
Why should we? That is why we are here.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce said a few weeks ago, "Boys, you will have to toe the line." He did not need to say that. They have been toeing the line for years. But he suggested to them that there should be no deviation. There has been ,no deviation, and there probably will be no deviation.
What about your own party?

I think it is only fair to say that when this bill goes to the banking and commerce committee, the government members will support it completely. Even if the hon. member for Greenwood or any members of his party decide at that late date that this company should not be incorporated their hands will be tied, because there is nothing they can do in the banking and commerce committee in the face of that kind of situation to change the provisions of this bill.
So I suggest that the Conservative party should have made a stand on this question. Particularly we would like to have seen them supporting the move to prevent further companies from getting into this field to carry on these high rates of interest and, more particularly, a move by the Conservative party to have the interest rates reduced.
The Liberal party is in favour of high interest rates. Even the move they made was a creeping step in the direction of an almost imperceptible reduction in interest rates. The Social Credit members had one speaker, I think, in this whole discussion or perhaps one or two others. They are probably going to vote with us, but there was no will to fight. They did not get in and help us. They just sat it out enjoyed the discussion and said, "We are not going to vote the wrong way. We are not going to be caught voting the wrong way, but we are not going to get in and wage a real scrap to get the interest rates down."
The attitude of the Conservative party, of course, should not be a surprise to anyone. It is precisely the same as the Liberal party,
(Mr. Argue.]
to help big business, to help the wealthy people through small loans companies to continue to fleece the ordinary Canadian.

I had not intended to say anything in this debate, but since a reference has been made to the Conservative party and since my hon. friend purports to judge and to look into the mirror and read it, I just wish to say that the Conservative party-and I assume all parties in this house-believe in the rule of law.
As I understand it, the rule of law has been well established in this country for many years, at least on this particular practice, namely that corporations seeking incorporation under a dominion charter, unless they come under the dominion Companies Act, come to this parliament and present their bills. Then they are given an opportunity to be heard, and the machinery set up for that purpose is the banking and commerce committee, to which this bill is going to be referred.
At this late date I certainly do not wish to see here the totalitarian control such as we have seen established in other parts of this world. I do not want to see the House of Commons adopt that practice, decide without trial and without judgment and say, "We condemn you without a hearing." Frankly, with respect, I think a great deal of this discussion about iniquitous interest rates has been completely out of order because we are dealing with the incorporation of one company and not with the general principle of this matter.
When the time comes for us to discuss that matter before the house we shall be prepared to take our stand on it, but we are not going to take the position-or at least I am not going to take it-that when the citizens of this country or any other country come before the parliament of Canada in accordance with the long established practice of the house, which has been in effect for 50 or 75 years, and when they present their bill, we will deal with it without a hearing.
If the attitude of the Conservative party is that these people should receive a hearing in the banking and commerce committee, it is one I am proud of and am prepared to stand by. I know nothing about this bill or the proponents of the bill. The committee may decide on this bill one way or the other. It may be that when it is reported back to the house the members of the house, myself, your party, any hon. member, will decide to take a certain position, but certainly we have not reached the stage in this country yet, and I hope we never will and I do not think we will-certainly if the Conservative party is in power we will not-where men are going to be tried and condemned without a hearing,

without a trial, and when the old established usages and principles which have made this country great and which we have inherited are going to go down the drain.
With all due respect I think it is much better to follow those principles than to have "Daddy Argue" or anyone else taking the child by the hand and saying, "This is not good for you. We know best; we are not going to let you do it." For that reason I am going to vote against the amendment and for the bill.
Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Conservative party is most revealing. It has been stated now that they will never again vote against the second reading of any bill-
If you want to read that into it, go ahead.

-for fear parliament would become a kangaroo court. I think we might refer to the incidents of last year when the Conservative party took a definite stand with respect to the defence production measure, and when they did get definite results.
This is a private bill.

I think the statement of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) that he knows nothing about the legislation before the house is just as revealing, because we have had a debate on this matter in the private members' hour-
I rise on a question of privilege. I did not say I knew nothing about the bill. I said I knew nothing of the proponents or sponsors of the bill, which is quite a different thing.

The fact still remains that we know enough about the functions of these loan companies in the field of supplying credit to the Canadian people that the members of the opposition at any rate should be well aware of the implications of these high interest rates so far as the Canadian public are concerned. If we are to be an effective opposition I think we should do everything within our power to prevent the continuation of this type of legislation.
I just want to say that I am in complete accord with the remarks that have been made by my colleagues in advocating a system of credit utilizing our credit unions which are set up in such a way as to deal fairly with the needs of the Canadian people without putting undue financial pressure on them and without charging the exorbitant rates of interest charged by these loan companies. I too am making one last appeal to those members

of the official opposition who some day want to occupy the seats of government to show some initiative now and support us in our effort to prevent the incorporation of this company.
